articles.title: Should I buy a Rumawip or other affordable housing unit?
articles.excerpt: Tens of thousands of affordable homes sit unsold while city prices hit records. Sean explains who these schemes really serve, and how they change the price of the homes around them.
articles.viewerQuestion: Is an affordable housing unit a good buy, and how do these schemes affect other buyers?
articles.answer: If you qualify and the location suits you, it can be very good value, because these homes are heavily subsidised. But Sean says the schemes have produced unsold homes while their cost is passed on to the open-market homes around them.
points: A good location makes it a bargain
The income limit is high
Open-market buyers pay for it

articles.title: Landed or condo: which holds its value better?
articles.excerpt: A reader assumes landed homes are guaranteed to appreciate while condos age. Sean explains why that view is hindsight, where condos win, and the price ceiling open landed homes run into.
articles.viewerQuestion: In a sought-after area such as Bukit Jalil, Hartamas or PJ, how would a condo's value hold up against a landed home over the long run?
articles.answer: Landed terrace houses do appreciate fastest, but "guaranteed" is hindsight. Condos in good locations grow a little more slowly yet earn far more rent, and older landed homes without security face a ceiling on what buyers will pay.

Open landed homes hit a price ceiling

articles.title: Should I buy now the condo I'll downsize to in 20 years?
articles.excerpt: A 36-year-old father of three wants a Bukit Jalil condo to rent out now and retire into later, but it needs RM150,000 down. Sean says no: sell the old apartment, regain two 90% loans and buy for cash flow.
articles.viewerQuestion: Does it make sense to buy now, rent it out even at a small loss, and move in at retirement? Or should he sell the Shah Alam apartment?
articles.answer: Don't buy it. Nobody knows what he will need, earn or be able to do at 56, and putting RM150,000 into a 70% loan for an own-stay project is the wrong tool. Sell the apartment, which frees a 90% loan for each of them, and buy for cash flow instead.
points: Twenty years is too far to plan a home
Joint names used up both 90% loans
At 70%, many units beat this one
The apartment is ready to sell

articles.title: Is buying an auction property worth the risk?
articles.excerpt: Auction prices can be the market's most genuine, but your deposit is lost if financing fails. Sean explains how auctions work and what to check before you bid.
articles.viewerQuestion: How does buying at auction work, and should a first-time buyer try it?
articles.answer: It can be a genuine bargain, but only for buyers with capital and knowledge. You pay 10% to bid and must settle the rest within 90 to 120 days, on a loan based on your winning price, so first-time buyers without savings are better off with new properties.
points: The loan follows the price you pay
Some deals can't be financed
You buy it as it is
Prices fall each round without bids

articles.title: Should I buy a property with my boyfriend or girlfriend?
articles.excerpt: Couples who buy in joint names find a break-up leaves both of them on the loan. Sean explains why he discourages it, and the arrangement he prefers.
articles.viewerQuestion: Should an unmarried couple buy a property together in joint names?
articles.answer: No. Joint names use up both partners' 90% loans on one property, and nobody plans for a break-up. If you must, set the terms out in writing; better still, buy in one name with the other as guarantor.
points: It wastes your 90% loans
Break-ups don't service loans
Joining names often means overreaching
One name, one guarantor

articles.title: I cancelled my booking. Was it FOMO, or the right call?
articles.excerpt: A 25-year-old booked a RM640,000 unit on a promised 15% return, then cancelled. Sean explains why that was right, and how to tell what you can actually afford.
articles.viewerQuestion: Was walking away right, or too conservative? And how does he stop worrying that prices will run away before he is ready?
articles.answer: Cancelling was right. The numbers only worked if nothing went wrong, and on his income a property of around RM300,000 to RM400,000 is the safer place to start.
points: A 15% return is a red flag
Student-style buildings are hard to exit
He could not survive a bad year
Time yourself, not the market

articles.title: I own four cars and want a fifth. Should I buy property instead?
articles.excerpt: A 28-year-old in Kuching with RM500,000 in fixed deposits, four cars and a baby on the way asks about landed homes, his rented-out house and his uncle's. Sean says fix the spending first.
articles.viewerQuestion: Should he keep his rented house, buy his uncle's, and choose landed or an apartment for his family home, and how much should he put down?
articles.answer: Keep the house he owns and, for a family with this many cars, a landed home makes sense. But on RM8,000 with RM6,800 spent each month, the real problem is spending: until he controls it and stops buying cars, the property questions don't matter.
points: His rented house is earning its keep
His uncle's house depends on the price
Cars lose value; homes gain it
Count cash flow, not units

articles.title: Is a cheap unit with good rent worth buying?
articles.excerpt: A buyer is offered two old units in central KL at RM160,000 each, renting to foreign workers at a 6.33% yield. Sean explains why cheap is not the same as money-making.
articles.viewerQuestion: With steady rent but little prospect of the price rising, is it still a good investment?
articles.answer: No. The cash flow works, but with almost no capital appreciation, a loan slot used up and only about RM200 a month to show for it, Sean says better deals are available and this one is not worth the headspace.
points: The yield clears the bar, just
There is almost nothing to sell later
It spends a 90% loan slot
Better deals are out there

articles.title: When should you stop renting and buy a home?
articles.excerpt: A 34-year-old renter is tired of moving and wants a home of his own, but friends warn him off. Sean tests the decision with his 85% rule.
articles.viewerQuestion: Should he buy a home in the area he already lives in, or keep renting and invest the money instead?
articles.answer: Buy it. He can afford it, he knows the area, and the unit would rent for most of its instalment if his plans ever change. That is what makes an own-stay purchase safe.

He is buying where he already lives
His foundations are in place

articles.answer: Check function before looks. Test every power point, water point, door and window first, compare the unit against your sale agreement, then move on to cosmetic flaws, and report everything through the proper channel.

articles.title: I bought at a discount. Why am I still losing money?
articles.excerpt: A homeowner who bought "at a good rate" during COVID now struggles with the instalment and cannot find tenants. Sean explains why a discount is not a bargain, and how to decide whether to hold, rent or sell.
articles.viewerQuestion: Did he buy into a money-losing development, and what should he do now?
articles.answer: A discount only helps if the price ends up below the area's median, not just below the project's old price. For a home already bought, the question now is whether to hold, rent or sell, and that depends on valuation, recent sales and the loan balance.

articles.title: I'm between jobs with savings. Should I buy my first property now?
articles.excerpt: A 27-year-old who left medicine for a master's degree has about RM380,000 saved and wants a RM400,000 investment unit in the Klang Valley, which he barely knows. Sean says research now, buy after six months in a new job.
articles.viewerQuestion: How should he choose between projects in unfamiliar areas, do view and floor level matter, and what should he do with his cash?
articles.answer: Wait. Without a payslip he can't qualify for a loan anyway, and a 35-year commitment needs a steady income first. Use the time to get to know the Klang Valley, then buy once he has six months of income from his new job.
points: Invest where people move for work

His cash is well placed

articles.title: Should I spend most of my cash on a fifth property before I marry?
articles.excerpt: A 27-year-old commission earner with four properties wants to put RM214,000 of his RM300,000 savings into a dual-key unit yielding 7.3%, a year before his wedding. Sean says the deal is fine; the timing isn't.
articles.viewerQuestion: Is this purchase a good move given his commitments and wedding plans, and is spending RM214,000 the smartest route to passive income?
articles.answer: No, not now. The property itself is a solid buy, but with renovation it would take about RM260,000 of his RM300,000, leaving a few months of spending on a commission income just before a wedding. Rushing because he doubts next year's income shows he isn't ready.

Paying more cash isn't smarter

Low valuations are normal in new projects

articles.title: Must your first property also be your home?
articles.excerpt: A 26-year-old bought an investment condo before a family home, and his future in-laws disapprove. Sean explains why investing first can be the smarter order.
articles.viewerQuestion: Is it better to buy a home first and invest later? And how should he explain his plan to in-laws who think he is being too aggressive?
articles.answer: Invest first and keep renting your home. Use your strongest borrowing years and your cheapest loans on property that tenants help pay for, and buy the family home later.

A home tends to become a big commitment
Judge it over 20 years, not in month one
Renting keeps the couple flexible

articles.title: Is it worth paying to furnish a unit before renting it out?
articles.excerpt: Spending RM30,000 to furnish a unit for RM500 more rent looks like a five-year payback. Sean explains how he weighs the cost, and why higher rent can add to a property's value.
articles.viewerQuestion: How do you decide whether furnishing a rental unit is worth the cost?
articles.answer: Furnish to let the unit faster or at a higher rent, but compare the right numbers. Against the roughly RM12,000 a unit needs anyway to be livable, a RM30,000 package costs about RM18,000 more, which buys time and design sense, and higher rent can lift what the property is worth.

articles.title: Is a guaranteed rental return worth buying into?
articles.excerpt: A reader has booked a hotel unit with a guaranteed 7% return. Sean explains where the guarantee really comes from, and why the exit is the bigger problem.
articles.viewerQuestion: He worries about the narrow access road, the operator choosing not to renew after nine years, and another pandemic. Is this kind of investment worth it?
articles.answer: Stay away unless it is a third or fourth property you can afford to lose. The guaranteed return is your own borrowed money paid back to you, the price is inflated, and the hotel operator is your only way out.

articles.answer: Budget well beyond the deposit. Legal fees on both the purchase and the loan, transfer stamp duty, valuation, handover deposits, compulsory insurance and yearly taxes all fall on the buyer, and a subsale costs the most upfront.

articles.title: I earn well but fear losing my savings. Should I invest in property?
articles.excerpt: A 30-year-old in Melaka earning RM24,000 a month, with RM450,000 in cash, fears one wrong move. Sean says buy a rental unit well within her means, and leave renovate-and-flip alone.
articles.viewerQuestion: Is she ready to invest in property, what should she buy, and should she flip houses or start a business instead?
articles.answer: Yes, she is ready, but should play well within her means: a rental unit of RM500,000 to RM1 million in a proven KL location, where the rent covers the instalment. Buying an old house to renovate and sell is where people without construction experience lose money.

articles.title: Why hold a property for 35 years instead of selling it?
articles.excerpt: A first-time buyer plans to sell after five years for a RM100,000 gain and asks why anyone would hold for 35. Sean explains the long equity game and why cash loses to inflation.
articles.viewerQuestion: What is the point of holding several properties for 30 to 35 years if they may be hard to rent or sell by then?
articles.answer: Flipping is hard now because developers already price in the gains, so Sean holds properties whose rent covers the instalment on zero down payment and lets tenants pay them off. Cash from a sale loses value to inflation while the property keeps pace, though there is no rule that you must hold to the end.

Cash loses to inflation
Older units still rent

articles.title: Can I buy a terrace house and run my tuition class in it?
articles.excerpt: A teacher in Kuantan wants a RM440,000 double-storey house to hold tuition classes downstairs and rent out the rooms upstairs. Sean says check first whether it can legally host a business.
articles.viewerQuestion: Should he buy the house to run his tuition class downstairs and rent out the rooms upstairs?
articles.answer: Only once he knows he can legally run a tuition centre there. Many do it in houses, but a residential title isn't meant for it, and neighbours, safety and licensing can end the plan. Without the business, the house has to stand as an investment, and its rent won't cover the instalment.

articles.title: How much housing loan can I actually get?

articles.viewerQuestion: How do banks decide how much housing loan you can get, and how can you work it out yourself before you start looking?
articles.answer: Banks use your debt service ratio: all your loan repayments, existing and new, divided by your net income. Work out your own figure first, so you only look at properties you can finance and don't collect rejections.

articles.title: Flexi, semi-flexi or fixed: how does housing loan interest work?
articles.excerpt: Most buyers compare loans only by the monthly instalment. Rena Choong explains how housing loans charge interest, why a lump sum belongs there, and when full flexi is worth its fee.
articles.viewerQuestion: How does a housing loan charge interest compared with a personal or car loan, and which type should you take if you want to pay it down faster?
articles.answer: A housing loan charges interest only on what you still owe, so a lump-sum prepayment cuts the interest and can shorten the loan, while personal and car loans fix the interest up front. If you will prepay or draw money back often, take a full flexi loan; on a semi-flexi loan you must ask the bank to apply any extra payment to the principal.

articles.answer: Most rejections are predictable: a DSR over the limit, recent arrears in CCRIS, a restructured loan, or a legal or AKPK record. Fix what you can and wait for a clean record before applying, because each rejection is visible to the next bank.

articles.answer: Either is defensible, because he has no urgent need for the money. First find out what the house is really worth. If a buyer offers above market value, Sean would sell, clear any housing loan and set up his child's education fund; otherwise holding it is fine.

articles.title: Should I buy my own place, or wait until I can afford it?

articles.answer: Parents can help, but use it to teach: pay the down payment and let the child pay the instalments, as savings for the future. Children should stand on their own feet; borrowing a sum and repaying it is fine, but asking for parents' savings to invest is not.

articles.title: Our family bought units through a property guru. How do we get out?

articles.title: Which taxes do I pay when I own and sell property?
articles.excerpt: Beyond the price, owners pay stamp duty, assessment, quit rent and RPGT, and income tax decides whether you can borrow at all. Sean goes through the five.
articles.viewerQuestion: Which taxes should a property buyer in Malaysia budget for?

articles.title: When does refinancing my housing loan make sense?
articles.excerpt: Refinancing can lower your rate, release equity, win back a 90% loan or clear expensive debt. Rena Choong explains each use, and the valuation and income tests that decide whether yours works.
articles.viewerQuestion: What can refinancing a housing loan achieve, and how do you know whether yours qualifies?
articles.answer: Refinance only with a clear purpose: a lower rate, cash from equity you have built, a 90% loan quota back, or clearing high-interest debt. articles.viewerQuestion: Should he use the rent-to-rent guarantee on a completed unit now, so its rent helps him buy a second property within six to 12 months?
articles.answer: No. Sean's problem is not the project or the scheme but the rush: on a RM3,000 income he is not ready to carry one property, let alone two, and a guarantee does not make an investment safe.

articles.title: We'll retire with six properties. What should we sell, and when?

articles.viewerQuestion: Should they sell the shop lot and cluster home, pay off the two apartments and buy a small unit in cash, or keep some properties for rent?
articles.answer: The plan is sound and would leave them debt-free with about RM3,300 a month in rent. But first decide what retirement means: stopping completely or slowing down. articles.title: Is buying a second property within a year too aggressive?

articles.answer: Not too aggressive for her income and finances, and the building rents well. articles.answer: The rebates are retail-price sales tactics that everybody gets, and a newer project only wins when the entry price makes sense. Let the existing unit run, use your second 90% loan slot only when you can afford it, and keep the capital a third property would need in global equities.

articles.title: Should I buy a Rumawip or other affordable housing unit?
articles.excerpt: Tens of thousands of affordable homes sit unsold while city prices hit records. Sean explains who these schemes really serve, and how they change the price of the homes around them.

question.context: A May 2026 news report found tens of thousands of completed homes priced below RM300,000 still unsold in Malaysia. Developers must build a share of affordable homes such as Rumawip, often 30% of a project's units at a ceiling price of RM300,000, while prices in prime areas keep rising.
question.text: Is an affordable housing unit a good buy, and how do these schemes affect other buyers?

answer.quote: People want affordable houses in the location that they want.
answer.summary: If you qualify and the location suits you, it can be very good value, because these homes are heavily subsidised. But Sean says the schemes have produced unsold homes while their cost is passed on to the open-market homes around them.

reasons.title: A good location makes it a bargain
reasons.body: Land and other costs are subsidised, so a RM300,000 Rumawip stands out in an area where open-market units cost about RM900 per sq ft. Market rent there usually covers the instalment, and one Rumawip unit in Bangsar South was auctioned at RM370,000.

reasons.title: The income limit is high
reasons.body: A married couple can qualify for Rumawip on a household income of up to RM15,000 a month and a single buyer on RM10,000, well above the median. If you qualify, Sean sees renting the unit out as your right, though he doesn't encourage it.

reasons.title: Open-market buyers pay for it
reasons.body: If each affordable unit costs RM450,000 to build and sells at RM300,000, a developer building 300 of them loses RM45 million and spreads it over the other 700 units. Some buyers now pay more for a project without affordable housing.

reasons.title: Compare it with open-market homes
reasons.body: A developer Sean interviewed points out that many lower-income buyers struggle to get a loan or find 10% down, while an open-market unit at RM350,000 may need no down payment and carries no restriction on renting or selling later.

actions: Check whether you qualify, and what restrictions apply to renting or reselling the unit.
Judge the location first: a subsidised home is good value only where people want to live.
Before buying to rent out, compare the rent nearby with your instalment.
When buying an open-market unit, ask whether the project includes affordable housing.
Compare against open-market units at a similar price, which may come with discounts and fewer restrictions.
articles.caveat: This is Sean's view of the market in May 2026, not advice on a particular scheme, and criteria differ between federal and state schemes. For the hardcore poor, he argues, government rental housing near the city would help more than ownership.

articles.title: Landed or condo: which holds its value better?
articles.excerpt: A reader assumes landed homes are guaranteed to appreciate while condos age. Sean explains why that view is hindsight, where condos win, and the price ceiling open landed homes run into.

question.asker: From Lau, a viewer who wrote in by email
question.context: Lau believes that because land is limited, a landed home in KL is almost guaranteed to appreciate over 20 to 30 years. Condos, on the other hand, age: however well managed, the building and facilities start to look old.
question.text: In a sought-after area such as Bukit Jalil, Hartamas or PJ, how would a condo's value hold up against a landed home over the long run?

answer.quote: The moral of the story is it's very easy to look back.
answer.summary: Landed terrace houses do appreciate fastest, but "guaranteed" is hindsight. Condos in good locations grow a little more slowly yet earn far more rent, and older landed homes without security face a ceiling on what buyers will pay.

reasons.title: Landed wins on growth, condos win on rent
reasons.body: Official statistics rank landed terrace houses first for capital appreciation, with apartments close behind; corner lots do best of all. But a two- to three-bedroom condo in PJ rents for about RM2,500 to RM2,800, a rate tenants will not pay for a terrace, because condos offer security, facilities and less space to clean and maintain.

reasons.title: Yesterday's safe bet was once the fringe
reasons.body: Subang Jaya, PJ and Damansara Utama were on the edge of development 20 to 30 years ago, and people who bought early apartments in Mont Kiara, Hartamas or Puchong made money too. Townships launch terraces first because they sell easily; condos come later, once land is scarce.

reasons.title: Open landed homes hit a price ceiling
reasons.body: Individual-title terraces sit on public roads that often become shortcuts, and guarding them depends on a residents' association. A household paying RM1.2 to 1.5 million earns around RM18,000 to RM20,000 a month and expects security. Sean believes unguarded landed homes will hit a price cap, and notes many older owners downsize into 1,500 to 1,800 sq ft condos.

reasons.title: Big landed homes are hard to sell
reasons.body: Luxury homes bought for RM800,000 years ago are now listed at RM3 to 4 million and struggling to sell. On a RM3 million home, a buyer needs about RM300,000 down plus RM300,000 to RM400,000 for renovation before moving in, which only the top 5% or so of Malaysians can afford.

actions: Decide first whether you want capital growth or rental income; they point to different property types.
If you buy landed, favour guarded or strata projects and avoid lots facing a main road or a likely shortcut.
Look at today's early-stage townships, rather than chasing locations that have already made their money.
Before buying a large landed home, ask who could afford to buy it from you in 20 years.
Consider renting the dream home and putting your capital into rental apartments instead, as Sean suggests.
articles.caveat: With unlimited capital, Sean says he would happily buy landed and commercial property in prime city areas; these trade-offs bite hardest for buyers stretching to afford. He also warns against copying US house-flipping advice, since Malaysian financing works very differently.

articles.title: Should I buy now the condo I'll downsize to in 20 years?
articles.excerpt: A 36-year-old father of three wants a Bukit Jalil condo to rent out now and retire into later, but it needs RM150,000 down. Sean says no: sell the old apartment, regain two 90% loans and buy for cash flow.

question.asker: From RC, a viewer who wrote in by email
question.context: RC is 36 with three children. He and his wife earn about RM20,000 a month together, and his side business brings in about RM25,000 more. They own a Shah Alam apartment bought for RM345,000 in 2014, rented at about RM1,600, and a RM1.3 million semi-D bought in 2023, both in joint names, so any further loan is capped at 70%. He is thinking of a Bukit Jalil condo to rent out until they downsize in 20 to 25 years, which would need about RM150,000 down and RM2,200 a month.
question.text: Does it make sense to buy now, rent it out even at a small loss, and move in at retirement? Or should he sell the Shah Alam apartment?

answer.quote: Invest in properties using credit. Invest in everything else using cash.
answer.summary: Don't buy it. Nobody knows what he will need, earn or be able to do at 56, and putting RM150,000 into a 70% loan for an own-stay project is the wrong tool. Sell the apartment, which frees a 90% loan for each of them, and buy for cash flow instead.

reasons.title: Twenty years is too far to plan a home
reasons.body: By 56 his income, health and family will all be different; if his side business grows, he may prefer somewhere quite different. A building also needs good management to stay in shape for decades, and the Urban Renewal Act uses 30 years as a checkpoint. Sean expects oversupply in parts of Bukit Jalil.

reasons.title: Joint names used up both 90% loans
reasons.body: Each Malaysian gets two 90% loans for residential property. A couple who buys every home jointly uses both people's slots each time, so their third purchase is capped at 70%. Selling the joint apartment frees a 90% slot for each of them.

reasons.title: At 70%, many units beat this one
reasons.body: With 30% down, which is the international norm, almost any KL project rents for more than its instalment. Putting RM150,000 down on an own-stay project only to break even is a poor use of that cash.

reasons.title: The apartment is ready to sell
reasons.body: Held for about ten years, it falls outside RPGT, which is counted from the SPA date. Sold at RM330,000 to RM350,000, it would roughly clear the loan, and a cut in interest rates would make it easier to sell as more buyers qualify.

actions: Prepare to sell the Shah Alam apartment, and ask agents to test the market now.
Keep the RM150,000 invested, or park it in the semi-D loan account to reduce interest if your bank allows it.
With your two freed 90% loans, buy units where the rent covers the instalment, comparing new, subsale, auction and bulk purchase.
If you want sole names later, ask the bank whether one spouse can refinance the other's share; that spouse's income must qualify for the whole loan.
Shop for a retirement home when you are near retirement; any time can be a good time to buy at the right price.
articles.caveat: If his wife has her own income, Sean encourages putting a property in her name alone. A joint name makes sense mainly for a spouse without income, who otherwise has no claim to the home.

articles.title: Is buying an auction property worth the risk?
articles.excerpt: Auction prices can be the market's most genuine, but your deposit is lost if financing fails. Sean explains how auctions work and what to check before you bid.

question.context: When an owner misses three consecutive monthly instalments, the bank can send the property to auction, a process that takes six to eight months. Auctions now run online, and many of the units on offer are newer ones from investors who bought more than they could carry.
question.text: How does buying at auction work, and should a first-time buyer try it?

answer.quote: This auction process requires a lot of capital.
answer.summary: It can be a genuine bargain, but only for buyers with capital and knowledge. You pay 10% to bid and must settle the rest within 90 to 120 days, on a loan based on your winning price, so first-time buyers without savings are better off with new properties.

reasons.title: The loan follows the price you pay
reasons.body: To bid on a unit with a RM360,000 reserve price you put up 10%, RM36,000. Win at RM380,000 and you can borrow 90% of that, RM342,000, not 90% of a RM500,000 market value. If the bank lends only 70%, you must find the difference.

reasons.title: Some deals can't be financed
reasons.body: A title under a private caveat can only be bought with cash, and some auctioned houses stand on land owned by someone else. Sean has seen bidders lose their 10% because no bank would lend.

reasons.title: You buy it as it is
reasons.body: Units are sold as is, often unseen inside. Unpaid maintenance fees can be large, up to RM160,000 on one unit left empty for years, so check whether the bank's terms say it will settle them. An occupant, especially an owner who has lost the home, can mean trouble.

reasons.title: Prices fall each round without bids
reasons.body: When nobody bids, the bank lowers the reserve, for example from RM500,000 to RM450,000, RM410,000 and then RM360,000. Genuine bidders can still push a unit back towards market value, so knowing which round to go in is a skill.

actions: Have 10% of the reserve price ready to bid, plus cash to cover any shortfall in financing.
Check how much a bank will lend on that particular unit before you bid.
Read the sale terms for caveats, who owns the land and who pays outstanding maintenance fees.
Use an agent experienced in auctions to arrange a viewing and find out who occupies the unit.
Set a maximum bid and stick to it; an agent can bid for you within your limit.
articles.caveat: If you have little more than an emergency fund, Sean says new properties are the better route. For buyers in their 30s to 50s with capital, auctions are worth comparing with subsale: they are no longer the shady, unregulated halls older buyers warn about, and many units are fairly new.

Sean checked his notes with Jeff, an agent who specialises in auction properties and whom the video recommends. The process is as described in 2021.

articles.title: Should I buy a property with my boyfriend or girlfriend?
articles.excerpt: Couples who buy in joint names find a break-up leaves both of them on the loan. Sean explains why he discourages it, and the arrangement he prefers.

question.context: Sean has seen friends' break-ups turn a property they bought together into a long, sticky problem. Couples usually join names because neither can afford the home alone, and bankers often suggest adding a second name to get a loan approved.
question.text: Should an unmarried couple buy a property together in joint names?

answer.quote: I will not encourage couples to actually buy property by joining names.
answer.summary: No. Joint names use up both partners' 90% loans on one property, and nobody plans for a break-up. If you must, set the terms out in writing; better still, buy in one name with the other as guarantor.

reasons.title: It wastes your 90% loans
reasons.body: Each person can usually get up to 90% financing on their first two residential loans; from the third it is normally 70%. Buying jointly uses both partners' quota on one property, while buying separately lets a couple hold up to four at 90%.

reasons.title: Break-ups don't service loans
reasons.body: If a couple stops talking, the instalments can stop too. The bank sends warning letters to both of you, and both get arrears recorded in CCRIS.

reasons.title: Joining names often means overreaching
reasons.body: If one income qualifies for a RM300,000 home but together you buy a RM700,000 landed house, you take on about RM3,500 a month for 30 years. Lose one income and the home is at risk.

reasons.title: One name, one guarantor
reasons.body: Sean prefers the property in one partner's name, with the other acting as guarantor on the loan if the income falls short. The other partner keeps their own quota for later purchases.

actions: Don't buy a property as proof of your relationship.
If one income can't support the home, look at a cheaper one before adding a second name.
If you do buy jointly, agree in writing, ideally with a lawyer, what happens if either of you loses a job, stops paying or wants to sell.
Consider buying in one name with your partner as guarantor.
articles.caveat: Sean has no objection to joint names between family members who trust each other, though never with a stranger, and a couple with clear written terms can make it work.

articles.title: I cancelled my booking. Was it FOMO, or the right call?
articles.excerpt: A 25-year-old booked a RM640,000 unit on a promised 15% return, then cancelled. Sean explains why that was right, and how to tell what you can actually afford.

question.asker: From Xiao Bai, a viewer who wrote in by email
question.context: Xiao Bai is 25, takes home about RM4,600 a month after EPF, has a car loan, and saves RM1,000 to RM1,500 a month with about RM20,000 put aside. He booked a RM640,000 leasehold unit in Bandar Sunway with more than RM30,000 cash back and a 10% rebate. The instalment would be about RM2,700 plus RM370 maintenance, and the agent promised a 15% return. After a month of doubt, he cancelled.
question.text: Was walking away right, or too conservative? And how does he stop worrying that prices will run away before he is ready?

answer.quote: It's a good move that you cancel.
answer.summary: Cancelling was right. The numbers only worked if nothing went wrong, and on his income a property of around RM300,000 to RM400,000 is the safer place to start.

reasons.title: A 15% return is a red flag
reasons.body: A good rental yield in Malaysia is about 5 to 6%. Anything far higher usually comes from student or Airbnb-style room-by-room rental, so ask whether the figure is gross or net. If a developer could really deliver 15%, it would charge more for the unit.

reasons.title: Student-style buildings are hard to exit
reasons.body: Buildings full of students wear out fast, so the sinking fund rises. Only other investors will buy such units, since families do not want to live there, and when a campus moves away, rents fall.

reasons.title: He could not survive a bad year
reasons.body: After the car loan, roughly RM3,500 of his income counts toward borrowing, enough for about RM400,000 to RM500,000. A RM2,700 instalment with little savings leaves nothing to carry the unit through six empty months.

reasons.title: Time yourself, not the market
reasons.body: Sean says any time is a good time to buy if you are ready. The cure for fear of missing out is knowledge: agents earn when you sign, not when you are still paying through a vacancy.

actions: Do your research before paying a booking fee, not after.
Visit about 20 properties in your budget; the sales pitches start to sound alike, which makes you immune to them.
Before buying, have six months of emergency funds, insurance, and a clear career path.
Work out the real price after cash back and rebates; after handover, banks value the unit on that lower figure, so selling early loses money.
Compare price per sq ft across areas. Bandar Sunway near RM1,000 can cost more than Mont Kiara or Bangsar South.
articles.caveat: Buying would not necessarily have been wrong for someone confident of a fast-rising income, such as in sales. Sean went all in on his first property at a similar income and nearly crashed, and says he would tell his younger self to slow down.

articles.title: I own four cars and want a fifth. Should I buy property instead?
articles.excerpt: A 28-year-old in Kuching with RM500,000 in fixed deposits, four cars and a baby on the way asks about landed homes, his rented-out house and his uncle's. Sean says fix the spending first.

question.asker: From TK, a viewer who wrote in by email
question.context: TK is 28, a project manager in Kuching earning RM8,000 a month and spending about RM6,800, much of it on four cars; he is eyeing a fifth for when his baby arrives. He has RM500,000 in fixed deposits and RM100,000 in EPF, and owns a double-storey house bought for RM418,000 with RM80,000 down, rented at RM900 against a RM1,450 instalment, though it could fetch RM1,200. He lives in his uncle's corner house and is weighing that house, a new RM700,000 to RM800,000 double-storey or a RM500,000 to RM600,000 apartment.
question.text: Should he keep his rented house, buy his uncle's, and choose landed or an apartment for his family home, and how much should he put down?

answer.quote: Why do you need four cars in the first place?
answer.summary: Keep the house he owns and, for a family with this many cars, a landed home makes sense. But on RM8,000 with RM6,800 spent each month, the real problem is spending: until he controls it and stops buying cars, the property questions don't matter.

reasons.title: His rented house is earning its keep
reasons.body: New double-storeys nearby sell for about RM620,000, so his RM418,000 house has likely gained. Early in a loan most of each instalment is interest; at RM1,200 rent, about 85% of the RM1,450 instalment, the tenant is effectively paying the bank's interest for him.

reasons.title: His uncle's house depends on the price
reasons.body: Bought for RM280,000 in 2015 with neighbours now at RM400,000, it has risen about 43% in ten years, and corner lots usually fetch 25% to 35% more. Compare his uncle's price plus renovation with RM800,000 for a new house in an area whose water and power supply he doesn't yet know.

reasons.title: Cars lose value; homes gain it
reasons.body: In ten years his cars will be worth half or less, while both houses he knows have risen. In Kuching renting is cheaper than owning, but the saving only helps if it is invested rather than spent on another car.

reasons.title: Count cash flow, not units
reasons.body: A better goal than owning many properties is positive monthly cash flow, such as RM10,000 a month across the portfolio. In Kuching, Sean would buy an apartment only if long-term rent, not Airbnb income, covers the instalment.

actions: Bring monthly spending down, ideally to about half your income, before buying more property, and don't buy the fifth car.
Raise the rent on your existing house to the market rate of about RM1,200 when the tenancy is renewed.
Ask your uncle his price, then compare it plus renovation with buying new.
Take a 90% full flexi loan and park spare cash in it to cut interest, after checking when your bank lets you withdraw it.
Move some of the RM500,000 fixed deposit into options that earn more, such as EPF, which pays about 6%.
articles.caveat: If the uncle would sell near his 2015 price, it is an easy yes. And Sean would buy an own-stay apartment only if nearby rents cover about 85% of its instalment, his rule for judging an own-stay purchase.

articles.title: Is a cheap unit with good rent worth buying?
articles.excerpt: A buyer is offered two old units in central KL at RM160,000 each, renting to foreign workers at a 6.33% yield. Sean explains why cheap is not the same as money-making.

question.asker: From Mrs. Y, a viewer who wrote in by email
question.context: Mrs. Y has bought a 1,750 sq ft own-stay unit from a large listed developer in KL East, still under construction. She is now offered two 425 sq ft units at RM160,000 each in an old building in Chow Kit, completed in 2000 and refurbished in 2020. They rent for RM1,000 a month, mostly to foreign workers, with a RM130 management fee, and she works out a 6.33% return before maintenance.
question.text: With steady rent but little prospect of the price rising, is it still a good investment?

answer.quote: Don't buy a property just because it's cheap.
answer.summary: No. The cash flow works, but with almost no capital appreciation, a loan slot used up and only about RM200 a month to show for it, Sean says better deals are available and this one is not worth the headspace.

reasons.title: The yield clears the bar, just
reasons.body: Sean's break-even is about 5.4%: a RM100,000 loan over 35 years at 4% costs about RM450 a month. At 6.33% the unit is roughly a point above that, and on a 90% loan of about RM145,000 the surplus comes to around RM200 a month.

reasons.title: There is almost nothing to sell later
reasons.body: Units like these compete on being the cheapest, for tenants who need them rather than want them, so the only buyers are other cash-flow investors and there is little resale activity. Even selling at 10% more in ten years, about RM176,000, the surplus of roughly RM2,400 a year barely returns the down payment. In the worst case it cannot be sold, and repairs after bad tenants eat the surplus.

reasons.title: It spends a 90% loan slot
reasons.body: Malaysians get two 90% loans for residential property. With her own-stay unit, this would use the second, so any better deal later could only be financed at 70%. Paying cash would be worse still: EPF pays about 6% with less risk.

reasons.title: Better deals are out there
reasons.body: She has not compared it against 20 other properties. Sean finds deals from branded developers with higher returns and no upfront deposit, so an old, cheap unit like this would need a double-digit return, 10% to 15%, before he considered it.

actions: Visit at least 20 other properties in your price range, across new, subsale, auction and bulk purchase, before deciding.
Ask a bank for its valuation first, to see whether it would value the unit at the asking price.
Don't pay cash for a property like this; compare its return against EPF at about 6%.
Keep your remaining 90% loan slot for a deal with both cash flow and room to grow.
For an old, low-priced building, look for a double-digit return of 10% to 15% before considering it.
articles.caveat: Sean's no rests on having better deals within reach. Cheap units in old buildings can make sense at a double-digit yield, though he discourages investors from low-cost housing meant for those who need it most. Separately, he says buying her own-stay unit from a large developer gives her more certainty of completion while building costs rise.

articles.title: When should you stop renting and buy a home?
articles.excerpt: A 34-year-old renter is tired of moving and wants a home of his own, but friends warn him off. Sean tests the decision with his 85% rule.

question.asker: From CY, a viewer who wrote in by email
question.context: CY is 34, single, earns about RM17,000 a month and lives frugally. He has RM180,000 in shares and cash and RM235,000 in EPF, and supports his mother. He rents a condo in Taman Desa for RM3,000 a month, and has had to move three times in six years when landlords took their units back. He is eyeing a RM850,000 project nearby with an instalment of about RM3,800, but friends say not to buy until he marries.
question.text: Should he buy a home in the area he already lives in, or keep renting and invest the money instead?

answer.quote: Go ahead bro, I really support that decision.
answer.summary: Buy it. He can afford it, he knows the area, and the unit would rent for most of its instalment if his plans ever change. That is what makes an own-stay purchase safe.

reasons.title: It passes the 85% rule
reasons.body: Sean's test for an own-stay home: local rent should cover about 85% of the instalment. In the early years most of each instalment is interest, so a tenant would cover that cost if you had to move out. Here, similar units rent for about RM3,000 against an instalment of about RM3,800, which Sean counts as meeting the rule.

reasons.title: He is buying where he already lives
reasons.body: The classic mistake is an emotional dream home far from work, such as a landed house in an outer suburb. The owner then faces hours of daily traffic or rents a second place in town. A home renovated for yourself is hard to let out, and a distant one is hard to sell. Taman Desa is central and CY has lived around it for six years.

reasons.title: His foundations are in place
reasons.body: Before buying a home, Sean wants three things settled: solid savings, a stable career and insurance protection. CY has all three, so the question becomes whether he wants to spend on housing, not whether he can afford to.

reasons.title: A home pays you in certainty
reasons.body: Some property is bought to make money; a home is bought to spend it. The instalment buys the security renting cannot: no landlord calling to reclaim the unit in your busiest month. Sean compares it to choosing a better car than the bare minimum, which is fine if you can afford it.

actions: Check what the unit would rent for, and aim for rent covering about 85% of your instalment.
Buy in an area you already know and that suits your daily commute, not a faraway dream location.
Confirm your savings, career and insurance are solid before committing.
Plan the exit now: if a better job comes up elsewhere, you can rent the unit out at market rate.
Treat renovation as spending on yourself. It makes the home yours but adds little to the resale price.
articles.caveat: If you want to build a property portfolio, Sean's own order is the reverse: buy investment units whose rent covers the instalment first, so your borrowing capacity stays intact, and buy your home later. His "just buy it" is for someone like CY, who invests elsewhere and wants a home for stability.

articles.title: What should you check when you get your keys?
articles.excerpt: Most buyers hunt for scratches and hollow tiles and miss what stops a home from working. Sean sets out what to check first in a defect inspection.

question.context: You have collected the keys to a new home, and the developer gives you a limited window to report defects. Most buyers walk in looking for stains and scratches, and miss the things that actually stop a home from working.
question.text: What should you check during a defect inspection, and in what order?

answer.quote: These are things that you cannot really live without.
answer.summary: Check function before looks. Test every power point, water point, door and window first, compare the unit against your sale agreement, then move on to cosmetic flaws, and report everything through the proper channel.

reasons.title: Utilities come first
reasons.body: Test every power point with a phone charger, plus the distribution board, doorbell and any water heater or appliances supplied. Doors and windows should open and close smoothly, and window seals should feel firm.

reasons.title: Water problems hide
reasons.body: Fill each sink and check the joints underneath. Pour water on bathroom floors, especially in the shower, to see that it runs to the drain. Look for stains on ceilings and around windows that point to leaks, particularly in landed homes.

reasons.title: Your sale agreement is the checklist
reasons.body: If the agreement promises laminated flooring in the bedrooms or full-height tiles in the kitchen, check that is what you got; a mismatch matters more than a stain. Some buyers even measure wall to wall, after stories of 900 sq ft units measuring 850.

reasons.title: Hollow tiles are more serious than they look
reasons.body: A hollow wall tile can eventually fall off; a hollow floor tile can crack under heavy furniture because there is no mortar beneath it. Straight walls and even floors are not a luxury at any price point.

actions: Bring a phone charger, your sale agreement and a measuring tape, and mark each defect with a sticker as you go.
Check the common facilities too: the building should have its certificate of completion, and the gym and pool should be working, not "under maintenance".
Submit defects through the developer's official channel; the staff follow process, so be thorough rather than confrontational.
Note the defect liability period, usually 24 months; leaks or cracks in that time are the developer's to fix. Structural renovation in a landed home can void claims for related cracks.
For a rental unit, prioritise whatever stops a tenant moving in; each round of repairs can cost two to three months of instalments.
articles.caveat: The quality of supplied furniture and finishes is usually not a claimable defect, because it cannot be measured. For a rental, cosmetic flaws rarely matter to tenants; for your own home, ones that bother you every day are worth pursuing.

articles.title: I bought at a discount. Why am I still losing money?
articles.excerpt: A homeowner who bought "at a good rate" during COVID now struggles with the instalment and cannot find tenants. Sean explains why a discount is not a bargain, and how to decide whether to hold, rent or sell.

question.asker: From Mr A, a viewer who wrote in by email
question.context: Mr A bought a 1,500 sq ft condo at Subang Park Homes in SS19 during COVID, because the price looked like a good deal. He lives there with his wife and child, but the loan and maintenance now cost about RM4,000 a month, and similar units listed for rent at RM3,000 to RM3,500 find no takers.
question.text: Did he buy into a money-losing development, and what should he do now?

answer.quote: Is it cheaper? Yes. Is it still expensive? Yes.
answer.summary: A discount only helps if the price ends up below the area's median, not just below the project's old price. For a home already bought, the question now is whether to hold, rent or sell, and that depends on valuation, recent sales and the loan balance.

reasons.title: The discount was measured against the wrong number
reasons.body: "20% below market value" usually means below a bank valuation or the developer's old asking price. The real market price is what similar units actually sold for. If the area median is RM900 per sq ft and a project drops from RM1,300 to RM1,100, it is cheaper and still expensive.

reasons.title: A quiet address does not draw tenants
reasons.body: High rents come from temporary demand: jobs, universities and tourism. A hidden residential corner suits a family, but most renters will pay more to live near a train station or highway.

reasons.title: The 85% test was never done
reasons.body: For an own-stay home, Sean checks that local rent covers about 85% of the instalment, so you have an exit if plans change. On a RM3,500 instalment that means rent of about RM3,000. Checking demand first would have shown the risk.

reasons.title: Who loses depends on when they bought
reasons.body: The developer profited at launch, and early buyers likely gained, but later buyers at peak prices often have not. Across the market, people who bought at the 2015 to 2016 peak are still underwater, while those who bought in the 2019 to 2021 dip gained equity.

actions: Ask your bank for a current valuation; it sets what your buyer can borrow.
Check the latest transacted prices in your project. If the last sale was a year ago, demand is thin.
Compare your outstanding loan with a realistic sale price. If selling leaves you owing the bank, decide whether to pay the gap now or keep paying monthly.
If you rent it out, check the competition: unfurnished listings with no takers leave room to win; furnished ones with no takers signal real trouble.
Next time, decide own stay or investment first, and check local rent before you buy.
articles.caveat: As a family home, the property is doing its job, so it is not automatically a failure; the pain is the instalment. On smart-home features, which Mr A also asked about, Sean thinks they add little to rent or resale and suit owners furnishing a home for themselves.

articles.title: I'm between jobs with savings. Should I buy my first property now?
articles.excerpt: A 27-year-old who left medicine for a master's degree has about RM380,000 saved and wants a RM400,000 investment unit in the Klang Valley, which he barely knows. Sean says research now, buy after six months in a new job.

question.asker: From Mr J, a viewer who wrote in by email
question.context: Mr J is 27 and lives in Melaka. He resigned as a government doctor to study a one-year master's in health tech, finishing in late 2026, and earns occasional income as a part-time property agent. Counting money market funds, cash, stocks and an insurance savings plan, he has about RM380,000, and he spends about RM2,000 a month. He is a client of a property investment club, can borrow RM600,000 to RM700,000, and wants a unit of about RM400,000 for cash flow, though he doesn't know KL or Selangor.
question.text: How should he choose between projects in unfamiliar areas, do view and floor level matter, and what should he do with his cash?

answer.quote: Don't buy any properties before 6 months income from your new job.
answer.summary: Wait. Without a payslip he can't qualify for a loan anyway, and a 35-year commitment needs a steady income first. Use the time to get to know the Klang Valley, then buy once he has six months of income from his new job.

reasons.title: Invest where people move for work
reasons.body: Sean always recommends main city centres such as KL, JB, Penang and Kuching, because fresh graduates head to the capital for jobs and rooms there are in short supply: about RM700 for a small room and RM1,200 for a master bedroom around Cheras. JB prices near the RTS link have already run up.

reasons.title: View matters only at the extremes
reasons.body: A KLCC or KL skyline view earns a premium for luxury and short-stay units, and a unit facing another tower 30 m away loses out. For a unit bought on rent versus instalment, view hardly matters, but floor level does in dense areas like Mont Kiara or Bangsar South, where low floors sit in the shadow of the next tower.

reasons.title: Completed units let you roll faster
reasons.body: A new launch can take four years before it earns rent you can show the bank. A completed or nearly completed unit can be let within months, and six months of declared rent helps you qualify for the next loan; developers also negotiate harder near completion.

reasons.title: His cash is well placed
reasons.body: Money market funds and savings keep him liquid while he has no steady income. With RM2,000 a month in spending, RM110,000 in the bank covers about four years, more than he needs as a buffer.

actions: Watch videos of KL and Selangor areas, then visit them: ride the LRT, walk the malls and get a feel for each address.
Join site tours if your investment club runs them, and view about 20 properties within your budget.
Stay within the RM400,000 range you are comfortable with, below the most you can borrow.
Plan who will manage the unit for you if you buy far from where you live.
Leave room in your savings for a wedding if marriage is likely in the next few years.
articles.caveat: Property investment beyond two or three units suits people who enjoy driving around, viewing buildings and dealing with strangers; if that drains you, stopping after using your two 90% loans is enough. Sean's thoughts on stocks in the episode are, in his words, not financial advice.

articles.title: Should I spend most of my cash on a fifth property before I marry?
articles.excerpt: A 27-year-old commission earner with four properties wants to put RM214,000 of his RM300,000 savings into a dual-key unit yielding 7.3%, a year before his wedding. Sean says the deal is fine; the timing isn't.

question.asker: From YG, a viewer who wrote in by email
question.context: YG is 27, earns about RM300,000 a year in commission and has RM300,000 in cash. He owns his landed home, an apartment and a low-cost flat, and helps pay for his father's flat; together his commitments come to about RM5,600 a month after rent. He is getting married next year and, unsure his income will last, wants to buy a dual-key unit near a mall for RM520,000, valued at RM480,000, with a 70% loan and about RM214,000 upfront, yielding about 7.3%.
question.text: Is this purchase a good move given his commitments and wedding plans, and is spending RM214,000 the smartest route to passive income?

answer.quote: I don't agree. Why put yourself in such a situation?
answer.summary: No, not now. The property itself is a solid buy, but with renovation it would take about RM260,000 of his RM300,000, leaving a few months of spending on a commission income just before a wedding. Rushing because he doubts next year's income shows he isn't ready.

reasons.title: Cash flow is what sinks investors
reasons.body: With about RM40,000 left and about RM8,000 a month in spending, he could last roughly six months if sales dried up. A property can't be turned into cash quickly: refinancing takes months and a sale seven to nine months before the money arrives.

reasons.title: Paying more cash isn't smarter
reasons.body: Every RM100,000 borrowed over 35 years at 4% costs about RM450 a month, so a yield of about 5.4% breaks even and about 6% covers maintenance and other costs. Sean would rather borrow the most he can, keep a year of expenses and six months of instalments per property in cash, and invest the rest.

reasons.title: Doubting your income means you're not ready
reasons.body: Sean learned in sales that income stays high when the work stays consistent. Buying now because the bank will lend on this year's income is a sign the plan rests on fear, not readiness.

reasons.title: Low valuations are normal in new projects
reasons.body: A newly completed project has few transactions, and banks know developers' prices include discounts, so a valuation below the price is common. Subsale units in good locations bought with 20% to 30% down often give positive cash flow.

actions: Park the RM200,000 in a fixed deposit, EPF or another stable investment, and treat it as gone so you keep working hard.
Rebuild a cash buffer that covers your commitments for at least six months before buying again.
Budget the wedding before committing savings to another property.
Get MLTA, MRTA or life insurance to cover your loans.
Look at what you spend each month; about RM8,000 is high for your stage.
articles.caveat: With about RM1 million in the bank, Sean says spending RM260,000 on this unit would be fine. And a buyer with no properties yet, and so a 90% loan available, should simply go ahead.

articles.title: Must your first property also be your home?
articles.excerpt: A 26-year-old bought an investment condo before a family home, and his future in-laws disapprove. Sean explains why investing first can be the smarter order.

question.asker: From Nick, a viewer who wrote in by email
question.context: Nick is 26, a dentist earning about RM20,000 a month, with RM100,000 in cash and RM100,000 in stocks. He has just bought a subsale three-bedroom condo in Shah Alam near his clinic for RM490,000, with his parents helping on the deposit. The instalment is RM2,000, maintenance RM330, and similar units rent for about RM2,200. He plans to rent a landed house nearby for RM1,600. His future in-laws think the couple should have bought their own home first.
question.text: Is it better to buy a home first and invest later? And how should he explain his plan to in-laws who think he is being too aggressive?

answer.quote: I support your move.
answer.summary: Invest first and keep renting your home. Use your strongest borrowing years and your cheapest loans on property that tenants help pay for, and buy the family home later.

reasons.title: The 90% loans are worth using early
reasons.body: Buyers get two residential loans at a 90% margin; from the third, it drops to 70%. Nick's unit needed about 17% upfront including stamp duty and legal fees, roughly RM85,000. As a third property it would need at least RM150,000. Spending a 90% loan on a home uses up one of the two cheap slots and much of his borrowing capacity.

reasons.title: A home tends to become a big commitment
reasons.body: On RM20,000 a month, the bank would happily lend Nick enough for a RM1 million landed house at around RM4,000 a month. After that come children, a bigger car and insurance. Buying the home first often leaves nothing for investing.

reasons.title: Judge it over 20 years, not in month one
reasons.body: Property is a long game. The aim of the first years is simply for the rent to roughly cover the instalment while the loan is paid down and the property gains value. A small monthly shortfall is the cost of holding, not a sign of failure. Compare who is wealthier in 15 to 30 years, not after the first year.

reasons.title: Renting keeps the couple flexible
reasons.body: A landed house renting at RM1,600 might cost RM800,000 to RM1 million to buy, at roughly RM4,000 a month. Renting costs far less, lets the couple move as their careers change, and spares them maintaining rooms they do not use yet.

actions: Once the first tenancy has run smoothly for about six months, start looking for the next investment.
Buy the family home later. Sean suggests putting it in the spouse's name, as he did, with extra life insurance so the loan is covered if anything happens to the main earner.
Hand the day-to-day work to a property management company so investing does not eat into your career.
Keep lifestyle spending low; spend on watches, cars and gadgets only from investment returns, not salary.
With family, listen for the worry behind the objection, but take investment advice from people already living the outcome you want.
articles.caveat: Sean's backing rests on Nick's unusually strong position: high income, solid savings and help with the deposit. With a thinner buffer, a monthly shortfall or a long vacancy hurts far more. Sean also says Shah Alam would not have been his own pick, but supports buying where you know the area well.

articles.title: Is it worth paying to furnish a unit before renting it out?
articles.excerpt: Spending RM30,000 to furnish a unit for RM500 more rent looks like a five-year payback. Sean explains how he weighs the cost, and why higher rent can add to a property's value.

question.context: Malaysian homes are usually handed over bare, like a car without an engine. Many owners ask how spending about RM30,000 to have an investment unit designer-furnished can be justified, when it may raise the rent by only RM400 to RM500 a month.
question.text: How do you decide whether furnishing a rental unit is worth the cost?

answer.quote: Using the lowest amount of investment to get the highest rental returns.
answer.summary: Furnish to let the unit faster or at a higher rent, but compare the right numbers. Against the roughly RM12,000 a unit needs anyway to be livable, a RM30,000 package costs about RM18,000 more, which buys time and design sense, and higher rent can lift what the property is worth.

reasons.title: Compare against the bare minimum
reasons.body: RM30,000 divided by RM500 suggests five years to break even. But a unit needs a kitchen cabinet, lights, fans, curtains, a water heater and other basics before anyone can live in it, about RM12,000 if you do it yourself, so the real extra is closer to RM18,000.

reasons.title: You are paying for time and design sense
reasons.body: Doing it yourself means managing contractors, taking leave for deliveries and having the eye for it. If you live nearby and enjoy that, you save money; Sean, who values time most, would rather pay. Furnishing companies typically finish in about 30 working days.

reasons.title: Rent can lift the property's value
reasons.body: RM400 to RM500 more rent a month is roughly the instalment on another RM100,000 of loan over 30 years. Where buyers value a property on its rental return, that extra rent can make it worth about RM100,000 more.

reasons.title: First impressions win tenants
reasons.body: Like a show unit in a sales gallery, a dressed-up unit wins on the first viewing. At the same rent, a tenant will pick the designed unit over an empty or semi-furnished one.

actions: Check the rents for bare, semi-furnished and fully furnished units in your project before deciding.
Spend only on what raises the rent or shortens the time the unit sits empty.
Skip personal touches like plaster ceilings and marble tops in an investment unit; save them for your own home.
Choose your contractor or furnishing company before you collect the keys, not after.
Do it yourself only if you have the time, the design sense and live close to the unit.
articles.caveat: For your own home the rule doesn't apply: there your budget is the limit. And whether the extra rent justifies the cost depends on your project's rental market.

Sean works with The Makeover Guys, a furnishing company the video promotes, so he has a stake in this advice. Figures are as stated in 2021.

articles.title: Is a guaranteed rental return worth buying into?
articles.excerpt: A reader has booked a hotel unit with a guaranteed 7% return. Sean explains where the guarantee really comes from, and why the exit is the bigger problem.

question.asker: From JH, a viewer who wrote in by email
question.context: JH has booked a 360 sq ft unit for RM700,000 in a hotel-run project near Genting Highlands. The developer guarantees a 7% return for three years, enough to cover the instalment and management fees with about RM1,000 a month to spare. After that, investors share 70% of the hotel profit for six years, and the operator handles utilities, furnishing and a refurbishment every three years.
question.text: He worries about the narrow access road, the operator choosing not to renew after nine years, and another pandemic. Is this kind of investment worth it?

answer.quote: I'm not a huge fan of GRR investment property.
answer.summary: Stay away unless it is a third or fourth property you can afford to lose. The guaranteed return is your own borrowed money paid back to you, the price is inflated, and the hotel operator is your only way out.

reasons.title: The guarantee is built into the price
reasons.body: A guaranteed rental return (GRR) is usually loaded into the sale price. A unit worth RM500,000 might be sold at RM700,000; you borrow the extra RM200,000 from the bank, and the developer hands it back to you as "returns" over three to five years.

reasons.title: You are paying city-centre prices for Genting
reasons.body: RM700,000 for 360 sq ft is about RM1,944 per sq ft, around what KLCC and TRX projects cost and more than Bukit Bintang. For short-stay rentals, the city centre also draws far more visitors than a tourist spot.

reasons.title: There is only one way out
reasons.body: A good investment property can be let long-term to families, short-term to expats, room by room or on Airbnb. This one only works as a hotel. If the operator walks away, as several did during the pandemic, you cannot live in it, rent it to locals or easily sell it, because buyers only want it for income it no longer makes.

reasons.title: The real return is thinner than 7%
reasons.body: Take off about 4% loan interest and roughly 1% in operating costs, and the margin is closer to 2%. Hotel use wears a building fast, so maintenance only rises. The operator is on a service contract it can leave after five years while your loan runs for 35, and business terms outside the sale agreement are not government-regulated.

actions: Work out the price per sq ft and compare it with prime city projects before trusting a guaranteed yield.
Ask what you would do if the operator left: could you live in it, rent it to locals, or sell it?
If you fear not finding tenants, buy below your limit instead. Sean suggests that someone approved for RM600,000 buy around RM480,000, so six empty months are survivable.
Keep your first two properties conventional; treat a scheme like this only as a third or fourth you can afford to lose.
Compare it with simpler options: fixed deposits, an index fund, or KL rentals yielding 5 to 6%.
articles.caveat: Sean stresses this is his general view of guaranteed-return schemes, not a judgement on this operator, and having a licensed hotel operator is a point in its favour. For an experienced investor with four or five properties, it is a risk you can choose to take.
articles.sourceNote: Summarised from Sean's full English captions for Asking Sean #259. The quoted answer is verbatim; everything else is paraphrased. Scheme terms vary by developer, so read the actual agreement before relying on any guarantee.

articles.title: What does buying a property really cost beyond the 10%?
articles.excerpt: Most first-time buyers budget the deposit and nothing else. Sean lists the costs that kept surprising him on his first purchase.

question.context: Ask what you need to buy a property in Malaysia and most people say 10%. Sean had exactly that for his first purchase, and the bills he had not budgeted for kept arriving one after another.
question.text: What else do you actually have to pay when you buy a property?

answer.quote: It's never 10%.
answer.summary: Budget well beyond the deposit. Legal fees on both the purchase and the loan, transfer stamp duty, valuation, handover deposits, compulsory insurance and yearly taxes all fall on the buyer, and a subsale costs the most upfront.

reasons.title: Legal fees come with more than one agreement
reasons.body: Developers often advertise a "free SPA", but that covers only the sale agreement. You also pay legal fees on the loan agreement with your bank, and owners of older blocks later pay again when the strata title is issued.

reasons.title: The transfer duty is the big one
reasons.body: Stamp duty on the memorandum of transfer (MOT) is due when ownership passes to you. Sean puts it at up to about 2% of the price, around RM14,000 on a RM700,000 home, and says few developers cover it.

reasons.title: Handover comes with deposits
reasons.body: Before you get the keys, a strata property usually needs about three months of maintenance fees as deposit, plus deposits for water, electricity and telecoms. A subsale also needs an independent valuation, paid by the buyer, before the bank will lend.

reasons.title: Some costs never stop
reasons.body: Banks effectively require mortgage insurance (MRTA or MLTA) before lending, and many require fire insurance too. Every year you also pay quit rent to the state and assessment tax to the local council; in strata buildings these often appear as a jump in the January or February maintenance bill.

actions: Plan for upfront cash well above 10% of the price, and more for a subsale.
Ask the developer in writing exactly which legal fees, and whether the MOT duty, are covered.
Set aside handover money: about three months of maintenance plus utility deposits.
Add mortgage and fire insurance to your loan costs, and quit rent and assessment tax to your yearly budget.
Estimate the legal fees and stamp duty for your price with the purchase cost calculator on this site.
articles.caveat: This is a 2019 episode. Fee scales have been revised since, and first-home stamp duty exemptions come and go with each Budget, so use these costs as a checklist and get current figures from your lawyer.

articles.title: I earn well but fear losing my savings. Should I invest in property?
articles.excerpt: A 30-year-old in Melaka earning RM24,000 a month, with RM450,000 in cash, fears one wrong move. Sean says buy a rental unit well within her means, and leave renovate-and-flip alone.

question.asker: From Miss J, a viewer who wrote in by email
question.context: Miss J is 30, lives in Melaka and works in sales, averaging about RM24,000 a month. She has about RM450,000 in cash, RM80,000 in stocks and a RM160,000 car loan, and spends about RM10,000 a month. Coming from an ordinary family with no backup, she worries that one failure would be hard to recover from, and wonders whether to flip a renovated landed house, buy for rental, keep her money in fixed deposits or start a business.
question.text: Is she ready to invest in property, what should she buy, and should she flip houses or start a business instead?

answer.quote: Don't even think about flipping.
answer.summary: Yes, she is ready, but should play well within her means: a rental unit of RM500,000 to RM1 million in a proven KL location, where the rent covers the instalment. Buying an old house to renovate and sell is where people without construction experience lose money.

reasons.title: A rental unit has few unknowns
reasons.body: In an established area you can see the selling prices, rents and neighbours before you buy, and work out the instalment and furnishing costs. If you can carry six months of vacancy, the worst case is lowering the rent a little until a tenant signs.

reasons.title: She can absorb a bad month
reasons.body: She could borrow RM2.5 million or more, but a RM1 million loan costs about RM4,500 a month, which her RM14,000 monthly surplus covers even if the unit sits empty. Sean prefers one RM1 million unit in a top KL location to two RM500,000 units elsewhere.

reasons.title: The contractor wins most flips
reasons.body: Without contacts or experience, contractors will exceed any budget: a RM200,000 gap between a run-down and a renovated terrace vanishes once wiring, pipes or the roof need replacing. Sean has never seen anyone outside the trade make money flipping.

reasons.title: Melaka's high-rise market is weak
reasons.body: Melaka has a population limit, abandoned projects and too many units built for short-term stays, which Penang and some building managements now restrict. Landed homes for own use still do well there, but for high-rise investment Sean points her to KL.

actions: Learn how each kind of loan charges interest, so you can tell a fair return from a scam.
Follow Sean's four steps: set your intent, check your loan eligibility, view 20 properties in your budget, then buy.
Start with a unit of RM500,000 to RM1 million whose market rent covers the instalment.
Have RM50,000 for furnishing plus six months of instalments ready at key collection, and skip auctions for a first purchase.
Keep your job; if you want a business, test the idea cheaply before putting savings into it.
articles.caveat: Buying a landed house in Melaka to renovate and live in for ten years or more is a different matter: bought at the median price, Sean is confident it wouldn't lose money. It is the quick two-year flip he disagrees with.

articles.title: Why hold a property for 35 years instead of selling it?
articles.excerpt: A first-time buyer plans to sell after five years for a RM100,000 gain and asks why anyone would hold for 35. Sean explains the long equity game and why cash loses to inflation.

question.asker: From Mr. C, a viewer who wrote in by email
question.context: Mr. C is planning his first purchase, a two-bedroom unit in a new Subang Jaya project with strong rent. His plan was to buy where rent covers the instalment and maintenance, then sell after about five years for a gain of perhaps RM100,000. He doubts the long game: older apartments decline, newer projects keep coming, and a RM500 to RM1,000 monthly surplus could turn negative during vacancies or repairs.
question.text: What is the point of holding several properties for 30 to 35 years if they may be hard to rent or sell by then?

answer.quote: Don't be too concerned of cash. Build the asset first.
answer.summary: Flipping is hard now because developers already price in the gains, so Sean holds properties whose rent covers the instalment on zero down payment and lets tenants pay them off. Cash from a sale loses value to inflation while the property keeps pace, though there is no rule that you must hold to the end.

reasons.title: Each RM500 surplus is about RM100,000 of value
reasons.body: A buyer can pay about RM100,000 more and still have rent cover the instalment. Sean's Mont Kiara unit, bought for about RM1 million three years ago with a RM4,000 instalment, should rent for RM5,500 to RM6,000, so he could sell at RM1.2 million to RM1.3 million, but would then have to find somewhere to put the cash.

reasons.title: Cash loses to inflation
reasons.body: Sean puts real inflation at around 10% to 12%, against about 6% from EPF, so cash shrinks every year. Property hedges inflation: rising building costs, higher wages and lower interest rates all lift the value of what existing owners hold.

reasons.title: Older units still rent
reasons.body: Older Mont Kiara units first sold at around RM380,000 to RM420,000 still yield about 5% to 5.5% at today's prices, because not everyone can afford new. Whether new beats old still comes down to location and management.

reasons.title: Tenants and the bank do the work
reasons.body: A break-even portfolio costs Sean about one and a half to two months of instalments a year in agent fees and repairs, roughly five years' worth over a 30-year loan. Five RM300,000 units renting at RM1,500 each would then pay him RM7,500 a month, for working on each unit once or twice a year.

actions: Buy only where rent covers the instalment and maintenance with zero down payment, Sean's strict rule.
Compare the price with the area's median so you never overpay.
Look at 20 different properties across the buying channels before settling on this one.
Use credit for property and put your own capital into other investments.
Judge any gain as a percentage of what you put in, not as a lump sum.
articles.caveat: The plan fails if the unit bleeds, with rent covering only half the instalment. Nor must you hold to the end: if life changes, such as moving overseas, Sean would sell. And if RM100,000 is large against your savings, taking the gain may be the right call for you.
