articles.title: Can I buy a terrace house and run my tuition class in it?
articles.excerpt: A teacher in Kuantan wants a RM440,000 double-storey house to hold tuition classes downstairs and rent out the rooms upstairs. Sean says check first whether it can legally host a business.

question.asker: From Mr TG, a viewer who wrote in by email
question.context: TG is 35, a government secondary school teacher recently transferred to Kuantan, where he now lives with his wife. He earns about RM6,000 a month, has no debts, RM130,000 in savings and RM30,000 in ETFs and stocks. His wife's own house, due in late 2026, is too small for classes, so he is eyeing the last unsold intermediate double-storey house in a completed Bukit Setongkol project for RM440,000, with the developer paying the SPA legal fees and stamp duty. He would hold it for about 20 years, then retire to Selangor.
question.text: Should he buy the house to run his tuition class downstairs and rent out the rooms upstairs?

answer.quote: I want to make money the right way, the legal way.
answer.summary: Only once he knows he can legally run a tuition centre there. Many do it in houses, but a residential title isn't meant for it, and neighbours, safety and licensing can end the plan. Without the business, the house has to stand as an investment, and its rent won't cover the instalment.

reasons.title: A home is not a licensed premises
reasons.body: A proper tuition centre usually rents a shop office, registers a business and meets fire and space requirements. Running one in a house saves on rent, utilities and licences, which is why it is common, but it lasts only until someone is hurt, something goes wrong or a neighbour complains.

reasons.title: Neighbours bear the cost
reasons.body: Classes of 30 to 100 students bring cars dropping off and picking up every evening, noise at night and heavy use of toilets and water. Some older KL houses on busy roads have been rezoned for business, but they still register as businesses and cost more to maintain.

reasons.title: Landed rent rarely covers the loan
reasons.body: At RM440,000 the instalment would be about RM2,000 a month, while local rents point to about RM1,500 to RM1,600, so the tenant would pay the interest and he the principal. In small towns people buy as soon as they can afford to, so rents stay low; landed homes earn mainly through price growth of about 3% to 5% a year.

reasons.title: Rooms for transferred staff can pay
reasons.body: In smaller towns, teachers, doctors and nurses on transfer struggle to find rooms quickly and will pay 20% to 30% more for immediate availability. His network of transferred teachers could fill the house room by room.

actions: Ask the local council whether you can get a licence to run a tuition centre in that house before buying.
Check rents for double-storey houses in the area; Sean would buy if it could rent for about RM2,000 a month.
Use your LPPSA housing loan if you go ahead.
Compare it with a unit of about RM400,000 to RM440,000 in KL whose rent covers the instalment.
When researching any home, find out what causes the area's traffic jams, such as schools, markets or highway bottlenecks.
articles.caveat: If he simply wants a family home near his wife's relatives to hold for 20 years, buying is reasonable, and the house number 4, which the agent offered to change, doesn't bother Sean. As a teacher on transfer, renting may also be the cheaper choice in a small town.

articles.title: How much housing loan can I actually get?
articles.excerpt: Banks decide with one number, your debt service ratio. Rena Choong shows how to estimate your own loan eligibility before visiting a sales gallery, and what CCRIS and CTOS reveal.

question.context: Sean's second step for every buyer is to find out how much they can borrow, yet many people avoid checking. In the second episode of his mortgage series, he asks Rena Choong, FAR Capital's head of mortgage, how banks work it out.
question.text: How do banks decide how much housing loan you can get, and how can you work it out yourself before you start looking?

by.name: Rena Choong
by.role: head of mortgage at FAR Capital

answer.quote: You should at least go and calculate your loan eligibility.
answer.summary: Banks use your debt service ratio: all your loan repayments, existing and new, divided by your net income. Work out your own figure first, so you only look at properties you can finance and don't collect rejections.

reasons.title: The DSR limit rises with income
reasons.body: Banks cap repayments at about 60% of net income for those earning under RM3,000 gross, 70% to 75% at RM3,000 to RM5,000, 75% to 80% above RM5,000, and up to 85% or 90% at some banks above RM10,000. Only debts in CCRIS count, such as housing, car, personal and PTPTN loans, credit cards and ASB financing; living costs and insurance don't.

reasons.title: A quick formula gives your limit
reasons.body: Take 80% of gross income as net, apply the bank's DSR limit, subtract existing repayments, then multiply by 250 for a 35-year loan. On RM6,000 gross, RM4,800 at 75% is RM3,600; less RM500 of debts leaves RM3,100, or about RM775,000. The multiplier falls with age, to about 230, 220 and 210, because loans end at around 70.

reasons.title: Your repayment record sets your rate
reasons.body: CCRIS shows the last 12 months, and each digit is the number of months in arrears; twos appearing more than once can sink an application. A weaker bank credit score still gets a loan, but at a higher rate, for example 3.4% or 3.5% instead of 3.3%.

reasons.title: Card balances count, not card limits
reasons.body: Banks count 5% of your outstanding credit card balance as a monthly commitment, and instalment plans count in full, so a big purchase just before applying can tip your DSR. Rena advises keeping card use below 30% of the limit.

actions: Get your free CCRIS report from Bank Negara (you register in person once), and consider a CTOS report, which also shows legal and trade records.
Calculate your DSR and loan eligibility before visiting sales galleries, and shortlist only properties within it.
Keep every repayment on time for at least the 12 months before you apply.
If your CCRIS is empty, take a credit card, spend a little and pay it off in full for about six months to build a record.
If you are self-employed or own over about 20% of a company, file and pay tax: banks will use your last two years of tax returns, not your payslip.
articles.caveat: Limits vary between banks and with Bank Negara rules; these are 2022 figures. A borderline DSR can sometimes still pass if you pledge a fixed deposit, while a poor repayment record can fail you even with eligibility to spare.
articles.sourceNote: Summarised from Sean's full English captions for episode 2 of his mortgage series with Rena Choong, FAR Capital's head of mortgage (August 2022). The quoted answer is Rena's own words; everything else is paraphrased. DSR limits and rates are as stated in 2022 and differ between banks. Sean is a customer of FAR Capital, not its owner.

articles.title: Flexi, semi-flexi or fixed: how does housing loan interest work?
articles.excerpt: Most buyers compare loans only by the monthly instalment. Rena Choong explains how housing loans charge interest, why a lump sum belongs there, and when full flexi is worth its fee.

question.context: Sean admits he rarely talks about the loan side of buying, even though rules on eligibility change often. In the first episode of his mortgage series, he asks Rena Choong, FAR Capital's head of mortgage and his own investment coach, how different loans charge interest.
question.text: How does a housing loan charge interest compared with a personal or car loan, and which type should you take if you want to pay it down faster?

by.name: Rena Choong
by.role: head of mortgage at FAR Capital

answer.quote: What you should do right now is actually first take a full flexi loan.
answer.summary: A housing loan charges interest only on what you still owe, so a lump-sum prepayment cuts the interest and can shorten the loan, while personal and car loans fix the interest up front. If you will prepay or draw money back often, take a full flexi loan; on a semi-flexi loan you must ask the bank to apply any extra payment to the principal.

reasons.title: Flat-rate loans charge all interest up front
reasons.body: A RM100,000 personal loan at 6% over 10 years adds RM60,000 of interest at the start, so you repay RM160,000, about RM1,333 a month. Paying it off early saves nothing unless you settle the whole amount.

reasons.title: Housing loan interest falls as you pay
reasons.body: On RM500,000 at 3.3% over 35 years, the instalment is about RM2,000, and early on roughly 70% of it, about RM1,300, is interest. Prepay RM100,000 and interest is charged on RM400,000 instead, so more of each instalment goes to principal and the term could shrink to 20 or 25 years.

reasons.title: Extra money in semi-flexi just sits there
reasons.body: Pay RM2,500 instead of RM2,000 on a semi-flexi loan and the bank still takes RM2,000; the rest is carried to next month without cutting interest. You have to register a prepayment by form, phone or email, and withdrawals need an application and a fee. Sean found his own surplus rent had been sitting idle this way.

reasons.title: Full flexi works like a cheaper overdraft
reasons.body: A full flexi loan lets you prepay and withdraw online at any time for a monthly fee of about RM10 to RM15. It suits business owners and the self-employed with uneven cash, and costs far less than an overdraft at 5% to 6%.

actions: Check whether each loan you hold is flat-rate or balance-reducing before deciding which to pay down.
Put spare lump sums against a balance-reducing loan's principal, not into a flat-rate loan you can't settle in full.
On a semi-flexi loan, save extra money into a lump sum and tell the bank in writing to apply it as a prepayment.
Choose full flexi if your income is irregular or you may need to draw the money back out.
Clear credit card debt first: it costs about 18% a year, against under 3% on Sean's latest housing loan in 2022.
articles.caveat: A fixed-rate housing loan protects you if the OPR rises but costs more if it falls, and banks offer it as a promotion rather than at your choosing. Rates, fees and prepayment terms differ between banks and have changed since 2022.

articles.title: Why was my housing loan rejected?
articles.excerpt: A rejected loan stays on record and makes the next bank wary. Rena Choong goes through the most common reasons banks say no, and what to fix before you apply again.

question.context: A rejection doesn't only cost you the property; it stays on record and makes the next bank cautious. In the third episode of his mortgage series, Sean asks Rena Choong which problems most often get a housing loan turned down.
question.text: What are the most common reasons banks reject a housing loan, and how do you avoid them?

by.name: Rena Choong
by.role: head of mortgage at FAR Capital

answer.quote: Please don't submit, wait until you fully settle it.
answer.summary: Most rejections are predictable: a DSR over the limit, recent arrears in CCRIS, a restructured loan, or a legal or AKPK record. Fix what you can and wait for a clean record before applying, because each rejection is visible to the next bank.

reasons.title: Recent arrears mean an upfront no
reasons.body: One month late is usually acceptable, but two or three months of arrears in CCRIS is treated as an upfront rejection. Settle in full and wait until the latest six months show zeros; late credit card payments are easier to explain than housing loan arrears.

reasons.title: Restructuring is worse than refinancing
reasons.body: Restructuring or rescheduling, stretching a loan because you can't keep up, signals distress and often leads to rejection. Refinancing to draw cash from a property's built-up equity is different, and a government-backed moratorium doesn't mark CCRIS, though applying to the same bank that granted it is awkward.

reasons.title: Legal records block even eligible buyers
reasons.body: Summonses and court cases, including against a company you direct, trade references such as unpaid phone or instalment bills above about RM300, AKPK and bankruptcy lead to rejection however good your income. A PTPTN arrears flag is lighter: settle the overdue amount, get the settlement letter, and you can apply within a month or two.

reasons.title: Every application leaves a mark
reasons.body: CCRIS shows pending applications, and banks notice when others have turned you down, so submitting to five or six banks at once looks bad. Rena suggests two or three at most.

actions: Check your DSR, loan eligibility and CCRIS before you apply.
Clear any arrears and wait for clean months before submitting.
Apply to two or three banks, not every panel bank at once.
If your DSR is borderline, pay down credit card balances, which count at 5% of what you owe, before applying.
If you have little credit history, use one credit card lightly and pay it in full each month, rather than collecting several cards.
articles.caveat: Banks weigh these things differently, so a case one bank rejects may suit another, and these are 2022 practices. With AKPK or bankruptcy on record, Sean's view is that buying property shouldn't be the priority for now.

The quoted answer is Rena's own words; everything else is paraphrased. Bank practices are as described in 2022 and change over time. Sean is a customer of FAR Capital, not its owner.

articles.title: My mother gave me her old house. Should I sell it?
articles.excerpt: A 53-year-old was gifted the Penang semi-D his mother bought 40 years ago. It barely rents, but he is attached to it. Sean says to find its true value first, then decide what the money is for.

question.asker: From Mr L, a viewer who wrote in by email
question.context: Mr L is 53 and lives elsewhere in Penang. His mother has gifted him an old semi-detached house near Green Lane that she bought about 40 years ago. Since a business tenant left, it has been hard to let; a friend rented it for about RM1,300 a month for a year. Similar houses nearby are listed at around RM1.9 million, several are for sale on his road, and he has about RM200,000 in stocks and savings and no commitments besides his child's school fees.
question.text: Should he sell the house, given its low rent, or keep it for its sentimental value and as his only landed property?

answer.quote: Property is a tool for us to achieve what we want to achieve.
answer.summary: Either is defensible, because he has no urgent need for the money. First find out what the house is really worth. If a buyer offers above market value, Sean would sell, clear any housing loan and set up his child's education fund; otherwise holding it is fine.

reasons.title: Rent is the wrong yardstick
reasons.body: RM1,300 a month is about RM15,600 a year, under 1% of a RM1.75 million house, so a fixed deposit looks better. But landed homes earn through scarcity and price growth: at a conservative 3% a year, the same house gains about RM52,500, which should be added to the rent before comparing.

reasons.title: Sentiment has a cost
reasons.body: Unless you live in it, Sean sees a house as a tool, and this one has done its job of giving the next generation a head start. Keeping it for sentiment means paying to maintain an old house, and the question becomes real the day a large sum is needed.

reasons.title: Sell when you don't need the money
reasons.body: The best prices come when you aren't forced to sell. Need half a million urgently and the first low offer wins, which is how investors find their deals.

reasons.title: Without a goal, nothing moves
reasons.body: With no retirement plan, education fund or other target, there is no reason to act, so the status quo wins. Sean suggests setting goals with a timeline, such as funding his child's university, alongside valuing the house.

actions: Get a bank valuation on the house, then ask local agents what it would sell for.
Check past transaction prices for similar houses nearby, so you don't sell for less than it's worth.
Work out your retirement plan and an education fund for your child, with the sums and dates they need.
If you sell, sell only above market value, then clear any housing loan and set aside the education fund.
Discuss the decision with your spouse.
articles.caveat: Sean was unsure whether Mr L's income was RM2,500 or RM25,000 a month, and his advice to consider selling assumes the lower figure. If Mr L plans to move into the house, or simply doesn't need the money, keeping it is also a sound choice; property is a good hedge against inflation.
articles.sourceNote: Summarised from Sean's full English captions for Asking Sean #305. The quoted answer is verbatim; everything else is paraphrased. The RM1.75 million value is Sean's working assumption, not a valuation. Figures are as stated in January 2026.

articles.title: I'm over 60. Should I still invest in property?
articles.excerpt: A reader over 60 is being offered short-stay units promising 9% returns. Sean explains why property loses its main advantage at that age, and what to consider instead.

question.asker: From Bernadette, a viewer who wrote in by email
question.context: Bernadette is over 60. People keep telling her fixed deposits are pointless and EPF returns may disappoint, and she has been shown developer-run short-stay projects in Bukit Bintang and KLCC advertised at 9.2% to 9.6% returns.
question.text: Should she invest in property at her age? Should she pay cash or borrow, buy new or subsale, and are these short-stay projects worth it?

answer.quote: A bit too late for real estate? Personally, I think so.
answer.summary: Probably not as a main plan. Property's big advantage is decades of cheap borrowing that tenants help repay, and at 60 that is mostly gone. Low-risk options paying a similar return, without the hassle or locked-up money, suit her better.

reasons.title: The leverage advantage is mostly gone
reasons.body: Banks usually cap loans around age 70, so the tenure is short. A RM500,000 loan at 4% costs about RM5,000 a month over 10 years against about RM2,200 over 35. Almost no RM500,000 unit rents for RM5,000.

reasons.title: Property locks your money up
reasons.body: Selling takes about four to five months for freehold and seven to eight for leasehold, which needs state consent. That is a problem if you suddenly need money for health or an emergency.

reasons.title: Other assets pay similar returns more easily
reasons.body: RM500,000 in fixed deposits at about 3% pays roughly RM1,250 a month; a property yielding 6% pays about RM2,500 but needs tenants, agents and upkeep. EPF has paid around 6%, and some Malaysian dividend stocks have paid more, with the freedom to sell part at any time.

reasons.title: Advertised short-stay returns rarely last
reasons.body: High returns usually hold only for the first years. Once a building proves profitable, more owners convert and a price war follows: in one Bukit Bintang project, nightly rates fell from about RM300 to RM120. Only investors buy such units, and authorities can ban short stays, as Singapore and Penang have.

actions: First decide whether this money is spare or what you will live on. If you depend on it, keep it liquid.
Compare any property yield with fixed deposits, EPF and dividend income before buying.
If you still earn and do buy for investment, Sean would borrow rather than pay cash, keeping cash for medical costs, with mortgage insurance so no debt passes to your family.
If you already own a short-stay unit, plan to sell while it is still profitable, typically within five years.
Be wary of returns quoted by the people selling the unit; get independent advice.
articles.caveat: For someone over 60 with spare capital, experience and other income, property can still work; Sean knows seasoned investors buying offices and land in cash at that age. For younger readers the lesson runs the other way: two or three paid-off properties by 60 can fund a comfortable retirement.
articles.sourceNote: Summarised from Sean's full English captions for Asking Sean #289. The quoted answer is verbatim; everything else is paraphrased. Rates and returns are as stated in July 2025 and will have changed.

articles.title: My ex and I own a house together. Should we sell or rent it out?
articles.excerpt: A couple bought a Puncak Alam home in joint names, then broke up badly. Selling now costs him about RM16,000; she wants to rent it out for five years. Sean says take the loss and move on.

question.asker: From Mr G, a viewer who wrote in by email
question.context: Mr G and his then-girlfriend bought a home in Puncak Alam in joint names for own stay, with an SPA price of about RM738,000 after discounts. They have since broken up on bad terms. The unit is now worth about RM650,000 against a loan balance of about RM656,000, so selling means covering a RM6,000 shortfall and about RM10,000 in legal fees. She wants to rent it out unfurnished for about RM1,500 to RM1,700 and sell in five years; he wants to sell now and is considering legal action to exit.
question.text: From an investment point of view, is selling now the right choice?

answer.quote: Own it. Own the mistake and move on.
answer.summary: Sell. Holding might work out better on paper, but not for him: two people who can't talk will fight over tenants and costs for years. About RM16,000 is a fair price for a clean slate, even if he pays her share as a farewell gift.

reasons.title: Numbers won't settle a feud
reasons.body: Both are accountants, but a spreadsheet won't persuade an ex who wants him out of her life. Each will expect the other to deal with tenants while the rent is split equally, and every conversation will start with blame.

reasons.title: He made the choices
reasons.body: They paid above nearby prices because it was a dream home, and the slow-growing location was there from the start. Accepting that the property and the partner were his choices is the quickest way out of the trouble.

reasons.title: Discounts were money from the future
reasons.body: A heavy discount lets you buy without the 18% in cash a subsale needs, but it means paying more than the market's price. Making that back over three to five years, as his friend in an earlier phase has, is a normal result, not a failure.

reasons.title: Unfurnished units rent cheaply
reasons.body: An empty unit only attracts tenants with very low rent. Owners who plan from the start to spend RM70,000 to RM80,000 furnishing it can rent for more, and the furnishing serves tenant after tenant, but that has to be planned before the keys, not after.

actions: Get quotes from lawyers for the sale costs and budget the shortfall to the bank.
Sell, even if you end up covering the full RM16,000 yourself.
Never buy a home in joint names with a boyfriend or girlfriend; if you must buy together, put it in one name.
If a couple can't afford a home in one name, rent, and each buy a unit of RM400,000 to RM500,000 whose rent covers the instalment.
If you buy to rent out, plan and save for furnishing before key collection.
articles.caveat: There is no RPGT to pay when selling below the SPA price. And to investors, Sean notes, sellers in this position are where good deals come from, which is why he always knows how much he can borrow.

articles.title: Is a leasehold condo with 60-odd years left too risky to buy?
articles.excerpt: A couple love a leasehold condo but worry it will be hard to sell with 60 to 70 years left on the lease. Sean says the lease is the smaller risk; buying together unmarried is the bigger one.

question.asker: From K, a viewer who wrote in by email
question.context: K and their girlfriend are from Penang, work in Selangor and earn RM15,000 a month between them, with only a RM700 car loan. They rent for RM1,280 a month and love a leasehold condo in Damansara Damai, built in 2006, for its space, quiet and reasonable price. They may move back to Penang or upgrade around 2036, when the lease would have roughly 60 to 70 years left.
question.text: Will a condo with 60 to 70 years left on its lease be hard to sell, even at the price they paid?

answer.quote: My concern is you buying with her as boyfriend, girlfriend.
answer.summary: The lease isn't the real risk. If the rent covers the instalment, they can always rent the unit out and wait, so they can buy if they like it. What worries Sean is buying jointly without an agreement.

reasons.title: Lease renewals can lift prices
reasons.body: Sean cites a Penang condo near Queensbay whose lease, with 30-odd years left, was renewed to 99 years for a fee of about RM1,000 to RM2,000 per owner; a local property expert told him prices nearly doubled. He sees little reason for a state to refuse to renew land under people's homes.

reasons.title: Freehold isn't absolute either
reasons.body: The government can compulsorily acquire any land, freehold included, for public works, and pays compensation based on market value. Freehold is now rare enough to sell at a premium, and this condo is reasonably priced partly because it is leasehold.

reasons.title: The real exit risk is financing
reasons.body: Once around 60 years are left, Sean says banks may not lend to the next buyer, which shrinks the pool you can sell to. That is why the rental market matters more than the title.

reasons.title: Here the rent covers the loan
reasons.body: Four-bedroom units were listed at about RM450,000 to RM460,000. A RM400,000 loan over 35 years at 4% costs about RM1,800 a month, and similar units rent for around RM2,000. If they need to leave, they can rent it out rather than sell.

actions: Check the rent for the same unit type: if it covers the instalment, your exit is settled even if selling becomes hard.
If you will need the sale money to upgrade, plan to sell sooner, around ten years in, rather than waiting until the lease is shorter.
If you buy as an unmarried couple, agree in writing first who can cash out and whether a buy-over is at market or SPA price.
Consider buying in one name: each of you keeps two 90% loan slots, while a joint purchase leaves you three between you.
Visit a few units before committing.
articles.caveat: If freehold is available at the same price, Sean would still choose it. His answer also relies on the rent covering the instalment; where it doesn't, the leasehold exit problem is real.

articles.title: Salaried, on commission or self-employed: what trips up a loan?
articles.excerpt: Banks judge your income by how you earn it. Rena Choong explains where employees, commission earners and business owners go wrong, and which records to prepare months ahead.

question.context: Banks look at income differently depending on how you earn it. In the fourth episode of his mortgage series, Sean asks Rena Choong where salaried employees, commission earners and business owners most often go wrong when they apply.
question.text: What mistakes get housing loans rejected for employees, commission earners and the self-employed, and how should each prepare?

by.name: Rena Choong
by.role: head of mortgage at FAR Capital

answer.quote: First of all, know which one is your income segment.
answer.summary: Know which income group you are in, because each is judged on different records: payslips and EPF for employees, commission statements and tax returns for agents, and company accounts and bank statements for business owners. Prepare them months before you buy, and never dress your income up.

reasons.title: Employees: the documents must match
reasons.body: The salary credited to your account should match your payslip, EPF should be paid, and you should be past probation; contracts shorter than six months are hard to finance. A sudden pay rise of around 50% needs a letter explaining it, and banks may call or email HR to check your job.

reasons.title: Bonuses count for less than basic pay
reasons.body: Some banks ignore performance bonuses or count about half, often only from multinationals and only after two years of history. A higher basic salary helps a loan more than a large bonus.

reasons.title: Commission earners need tax returns
reasons.body: Banks want six months of commission statements plus your latest tax return, so new agents who haven't filed one struggle. If income swings by more than about 30% from month to month, some banks count only half of the six-month average.

reasons.title: Business owners are judged by the company
reasons.body: Most banks want the company registered for at least two years, a busy bank account, month-end balances that aren't too low (Rena treats under RM50,000 as low), and invoices for large one-off credits. Declaring losses to cut tax shows up in CTOS and works against you.

actions: Keep a monthly file of payslips, bank statements and tax returns, so you can apply when a good deal appears.
If you are employed, wait until you are confirmed, and get a letter from HR for any big salary increase.
If you earn commission or run a business, file and pay tax on your full income for at least the last year or two.
If your income is complicated, ask a mortgage adviser who knows which banks favour your profile.
Never use arranged employment or inflated payslips to qualify; Rena and Sean call it fraud.
articles.caveat: Bank policies vary widely, especially for side income and mixed earnings, and these are 2022 practices. Income from investments or trading counts only once it is declared for tax, so declare it before you apply.

articles.title: Is "location, location, location" still the rule?
articles.excerpt: A young investor has shortlisted Bangsar South by its rental demand. Sean argues that location is not what makes you money; the price you pay against the area median is.

question.asker: From An anonymous viewer who wrote in by email
question.context: The reader is 26, works for a multinational in Johor and takes home about RM9,500 a month. He already owns a PJ serviced apartment whose RM2,200 rent nearly covers its RM2,300 instalment, plus RM150,000 in US stocks and RM50,000 in spare cash. He has shortlisted Bangsar South for its rental demand and compared units on tenure, age, size, furnishing, distance to the LRT and price per square foot.
question.text: Is "location, location, location" still the rule? Should he pay more for a newer project or buy an older subsale, and could he fund it with a 36-month interest-free credit card plan?

answer.quote: That's just a very cool way to say things in a lazy manner.
answer.summary: Location matters less than people think. Most KL areas will end up with the same amenities, so your profit is decided by your entry price: buy below the area's median price.

reasons.title: Entry price decides profit, not the postcode
reasons.body: In time, every KL location gets a mall, schools, a hospital and parks. What separates a good buy is paying below the local median. Sean would rather buy in Rawang at RM480 per sq ft where the median is RM600 than in KL Sentral at RM800 where the median is RM700.

reasons.title: High rent follows temporary demand
reasons.body: Strong rents come from people posted somewhere for two or three years, so job hubs such as Mont Kiara, KL Sentral, KLCC and Bangsar South do well, with Cheras, Subang and Bukit Jalil rising. In purely residential areas, long-term residents would rather buy than pay rent above an instalment, so yields are lower.

reasons.title: New costs more but ages better
reasons.body: Malaysian building and strata rules mean an old apartment's layout cannot be changed. Newer projects have brighter rooms, better ventilation and corridors, so they tend to appreciate more, while older ones usually yield more. Decide which you are buying for.

reasons.title: A subsale starts earning sooner
reasons.body: With cash on hand, a completed subsale lets you negotiate on price and collect rent within about nine months of signing. A new launch ties up one of your loan slots for three to four years before it earns anything.

actions: Check every shortlisted unit's price per sq ft against the area median, and only buy below it.
Decide whether you want rental yield or capital growth before choosing between an older subsale and a newer project.
Skip the interest-free credit card plan if you can pay cash. Sean would take the safe route rather than leave no room for error.
Visit the buildings in person; a spreadsheet cannot show you what a project is really like.
Avoid low-cost flats bought purely for yield. Sean will not buy social housing meant for people in need.
articles.caveat: Sean holds any unit whose rent covers its instalment for the full 30 years, while others prefer to sell after seven or eight years, once yields fall from about 7% to 5.5%. Both can work. Sean also mentions buying through FAR Capital, a deal-sourcing service he pays to use, for readers short on research time.

articles.title: I'm a civil servant. How should I use my LPPSA housing loan?
articles.excerpt: Civil servants can borrow from LPPSA on top of the usual bank loans. Rena Choong explains why the order you use them in matters, and the catches in LPPSA's terms.

question.context: Civil servants can borrow from LPPSA, the government's housing loan scheme for public-sector staff, on top of the bank loans everyone else uses. In the fifth episode of his mortgage series, Sean asks Rena Choong how it works and when to use it.
question.text: How does an LPPSA loan differ from a bank loan, and when should a civil servant use it?

by.name: Rena Choong
by.role: head of mortgage at FAR Capital

answer.quote: Please don't use it for your first and second.
answer.summary: Use your two 90% bank loans first and keep LPPSA, which can finance 100%, for the third property. LPPSA repayments come off your payslip, so using it first lowers the net income banks see and leaves your next bank loan at 70%.

reasons.title: The order changes your margins
reasons.body: LPPSA doesn't appear in CCRIS, but its deduction shows on your payslip, and banks count it. Banks give 90% on your first two residential loans; use LPPSA first and your third property needs a 70% bank loan, whereas two bank loans first leave LPPSA's 100% for the third.

reasons.title: A fixed 4% over a very long term
reasons.body: LPPSA charges a fixed 4%, close to banks' best rates of 3.7% to 3.8% at the time, and for those on the pension scheme it can run to age 90, against 70 or 75 at banks. But takaful cover is compulsory for the whole term, which becomes expensive if you borrow after about 45.

reasons.title: Full instalments start after two years
reasons.body: On a property under construction, LPPSA deductions begin about 24 months after you borrow, and from then you pay the full instalment even if the building isn't finished. A bank charges only progressive interest on what it has released, so a long or delayed project costs more under LPPSA.

reasons.title: LPPSA has its own limits
reasons.body: The maximum LPPSA loan is RM750,000 including takaful, and valuations by the government valuer tend to be conservative. If you leave government service, you must refinance with a commercial bank, and banks often don't recognise a civil servant's side income.

actions: Check how much you can borrow with LPPSA's own online calculator, which works from a fixed table by gross income.
Take your first two residential properties with bank loans, and save LPPSA for the third.
Prefer completed properties or short builds when using LPPSA, since full instalments start after 24 months.
Apply online and submit the physical documents yourself, or pay a runner to handle them.
Send loan documents only through a company's official channels, never to a personal email address, and guard your IC number.
articles.caveat: This only suits civil servants whose income comfortably covers several loans and whose properties earn rent; Sean warns against borrowing more just because the facility exists. Rates and limits are as stated in November 2022.
articles.sourceNote: Summarised from Sean's full English captions for episode 5 of his mortgage series with Rena Choong, FAR Capital's head of mortgage (November 2022). The quoted answer is Rena's own words; everything else is paraphrased. LPPSA rates and limits are as stated in 2022, so check LPPSA's current terms. Sean is a customer of FAR Capital, not its owner.

articles.title: My unit has no strata title yet. Does it matter?
articles.excerpt: A high-rise unit still under the master title can be harder to sell and finance. Sean explains what a strata title proves, and what to ask about parcels and share units.

question.asker: From a viewer hunting for his first property
question.context: He found a high-rise unit whose strata title had yet to be issued, so it was still under the master title. Each plot of land has one title; when a developer builds, say, 300 units on it, each unit should later get its own strata title.
question.text: What does it mean when a unit is still under the master title, and can it still be sold?

answer.quote: Yes, but you need the consent of the land owner.
answer.summary: It means you can't yet prove ownership of your own unit. You can still sell it, but only with the consent of the land owner, usually the developer, which adds a hurdle for buyers and banks. A strata title removes it.

reasons.title: The title is the unit's birth certificate
reasons.body: A strata title proves which unit in which block is yours. Without it, banks find it harder to establish the owner, which complicates financing and sales. Sean expects units with strata titles to fetch slightly higher prices because the paperwork is easier.

reasons.title: A missing title may be delay or bad news
reasons.body: It may simply be in progress, since issuing titles takes time and newer strata rules push developers to issue them soon after handover. But it can also mean the developer won't follow through or has gone bankrupt.

reasons.title: Ownership gives you a vote
reasons.body: Strata owners take part in the joint management body or management corporation, which sets maintenance fees and may not make a profit. Votes are weighted by share units, increasingly used instead of floor area.

reasons.title: Parcels decide what you pay for
reasons.body: A strata unit has a main parcel, the unit itself, and accessory parcels such as a car park or air-conditioner ledge. Common property like the pool serves everyone, while mixed developments may have limited common property for offices or residents only. All of this shapes maintenance fees.

actions: Before buying a completed high-rise unit, ask whether its strata title has been issued.
If not, ask why and how long the developer expects it to take, and how it gives consent for a sale.
Ask what your accessory parcels include, such as car parks and air-conditioner ledges.
Ask how share units are calculated, since they set your voting weight and maintenance share.
articles.caveat: This applies to high-rise and other stratified developments; a landed house on its own individual title is a different case. A unit still waiting for its strata title soon after completion is normal; the concern is when it never arrives.
articles.sourceNote: Summarised from Sean's full English captions for this July 2018 episode. The quoted answer is verbatim; everything else is paraphrased. The captions are unclear in places, so only clearly stated points are included. Strata rules have changed since 2018, so check the current position with your lawyer.

articles.title: A baby is coming. Move in, or rent out our first home?
articles.excerpt: A couple bought a new condo as their first home, but their first child arrives as it is handed over. Sean explains why he would rent it out and stay with family for now.

question.asker: From JC, a viewer who wrote in by email
question.context: JC, 32, and his wife are expecting their first child in May 2027. They take home about RM15,000 a month, have more than six months of emergency funds and around RM100,000 invested. In 2023 they bought a River Park unit in Bangsar South for about RM700,000, roughly RM900 per sq ft, at RM3,000 a month, as their first home. Handover has slipped into 2027, and they live with his parents in Kepong.
question.text: With a baby coming, should they stay with his parents, rent the unit out and live elsewhere, or move in as planned despite the renovation noise from 1,300 new neighbours?

answer.quote: Just keep it as an investment unit.
answer.summary: Stay with family for the first year or two and rent River Park out from handover. Treat it as an investment, and move somewhere that suits the baby later, renting if you need to.

reasons.title: A newborn needs hands more than space
reasons.body: The first six months mean broken sleep. Grandparents nearby give parents a few hours' break and can step in for daycare pickups. Sean moved out of his in-laws' home only when his son was about a year old.

reasons.title: The unit works better as a rental
reasons.body: To Sean, River Park looks more like an investment property than a family home. With the entry price on the high side, it needs rent of about RM3,300 (the RM3,000 instalment plus about RM300 maintenance) to break even, and the coming MRT3 station could lift rents.

reasons.title: 1,300 new units is less of a threat than it looks
reasons.body: Some 8,000 to 10,000 units are coming to the surrounding areas over five years. The way to compete is to be the best unit: Sean estimates only about 5% of owners spend RM50,000 to RM60,000 furnishing a rental properly.

reasons.title: Moving in now means a year of drilling
reasons.body: In a new block, most owners renovate in the first year, so the corridor noise is constant. That is a hard start for a newborn.

actions: Count the completion date from your sale agreement, not the agent's promises; delay compensation runs from your own signing date.
Furnish the unit well enough to stand out and attract the best-paying tenant.
Keep about six months of instalments in reserve for this unit.
Sort out life insurance and mortgage insurance now; Sean finds MRTA the simplest if you might lose track of separate policies.
Do not rush the next purchase; Sean would not buy again in the first three years of parenthood.
articles.caveat: If living with parents strains things once the baby arrives, renting a place near work or daycare is a reasonable next step while the unit stays rented. When you eventually sell, check the gains tax rules for that year; Sean notes residential property held over five years from signing generally pays none, but rules change with each Budget.

articles.title: Should you buy new from a developer or a subsale?
articles.excerpt: A new launch and a subsale unit can cost the same on paper but ask for very different cash, time and risk. Sean explains who each one suits.

question.context: A new launch from a developer and a subsale unit from an existing owner can carry similar prices, yet they demand very different amounts of cash, waiting time and risk. Many buyers choose on price alone.
question.text: Should you buy new from a developer, or a subsale unit?

answer.quote: I can immediately start renting out.
answer.summary: It depends on your cash and experience. Investors with capital should favour a subsale, where you can see the real condition and rent from day one. First-time buyers short on cash are better served by a new launch.

reasons.title: A new launch needs far less cash upfront
reasons.body: Developer packages and rebates can let you in with 1 to 2% in cash: about RM8,000 on an RM800,000 unit. Sean estimates a RM600,000 subsale needs around RM80,000, covering a 10% deposit plus your own lawyer, valuer, stamp duty and transfer costs.

reasons.title: Developers handle the paperwork
reasons.body: A developer lines up the bankers, lawyers, valuers and approvals for you. For a first-time buyer unfamiliar with the process, that convenience matters; a subsale means coordinating it all yourself.

reasons.title: With a subsale, what you see is what you get
reasons.body: You can see the actual condition, the neighbours, the schools and the train station that already exists. A new launch is sold on plans, and facilities marked "proposed" may arrive late or not at all.

reasons.title: A subsale earns rent straight away
reasons.body: New launches take about two years to complete for landed homes and three to five for large high-rises. A big project can also hand over thousands of units at once, all competing for the same tenants.

actions: Start from your intent and your cash: limited cash and a first purchase point to a new launch; capital and experience point to a subsale.
With a new launch, separate what is approved from what is only "proposed" in the brochure.
With a subsale, check current rents and condition, and budget about 10% plus fees in cash.
If you need somewhere to live soon, choose a completed unit; a new launch may take years.
In a large new project, consider how many units will hit the rental market at handover.
articles.caveat: This is a 2017 episode, so treat the cash figures as illustrations: developer packages vary, so get what is offered in writing. If you already own a home and can wait, a new launch can still suit an investor willing to hold through construction.
articles.sourceNote: Summarised from Sean's English captions for this August 2017 episode. The quoted answer is verbatim; everything else is paraphrased. Parts of the older automatic captions are unclear, so only clearly stated points are included.

articles.title: Can I really buy a property with no money down?
articles.excerpt: Discounts, rebates and cash backs promise a property with no capital. Sean explains how these deals work, and why you still need cash and a strong loan profile to use them.

question.context: Buyers used to need 10% down, and Sean needed nearly RM50,000 to buy his first RM300,000 property. Today developers offer discounts of at least 10%, cash backs and RM500 booking fees, and many young buyers take that to mean property needs no money at all.
question.text: Is a no money down deal really free of money, and who can use one?

answer.quote: You still need money even though it's a zero money down deal.
answer.summary: Only by the end of the deal. You still need cash to get it started and the income to qualify for a loan at the right margin; the "zero" appears only once the bank releases the loan and refunds what you paid.

reasons.title: Subsale deals still need 10% upfront
reasons.body: In a subsale, the deal rests on the gap between the bank's valuation and the price, so that a 90% loan covers the whole purchase. You still pay a 2% earnest deposit and the rest of the 10% at the SPA, refunded only after the loan is released, and you usually cover any extra RPGT the seller pays.

reasons.title: Developers want more than RM500
reasons.body: Established developers usually ask 1% to 3% upfront, often RM5,000 to RM15,000. It is refunded once construction reaches a stage the bank pays for, such as when the foundation is done.

reasons.title: It all depends on a 90% loan
reasons.body: These deals work only if your age, income and record get you a 90% loan. From the third property the margin drops to 70%, which is why discounts of 25% to 30% and cash backs appeared: they fill that gap.

reasons.title: Infinite returns didn't save the old deals
reasons.body: About 11 or 12 years earlier, Sean saw investment clubs sell bulk-purchase units on "infinite returns", since any return divided by zero capital is infinite. None of those properties succeeded.

actions: Keep cash for the booking fee, earnest deposit and balance of the 10%, even when a deal is billed as zero down.
Check that you qualify for a 90% loan before relying on a discount or cash back.
Decide in advance what the capital you keep will do, such as investing it, rather than letting it fund your lifestyle.
Be wary of anyone promising several properties on a fresh graduate's salary.
articles.caveat: Some wealthier buyers, often business owners, prefer to pay 30% to 50% down and borrow less, to save interest or park their cash; Sean sees no right or wrong in that. Using as little of your own money as possible suits someone building several properties, not someone stretching to buy one.
articles.sourceNote: Summarised from Sean's full English captions for this July 2021 episode. The quoted answer is verbatim; everything else is paraphrased. Loan margins and developer practices are as described in 2021.

articles.title: Is an older Bukit Jalil apartment a good first investment?
articles.excerpt: A 33-year-old with savings and no debts wants a well-kept 1990s subsale unit in Bukit Jalil whose rent already covers the loan. Sean calls it safe, but would look for better options first.

question.asker: From Miss L, a viewer who wrote in by email
question.context: Miss L is 33, earns RM10,000 to RM13,000 a month, has about RM60,000 in savings, RM50,000 invested and no debts besides RM700 a month in insurance. She once lived as a student in an apartment block built in the late 1990s in Bukit Jalil, and an owner is selling a well-kept 1,200 sq ft unit there for RM455,000, about RM371 per sq ft. Similar units rent for about RM2,200 a month.
question.text: Is this subsale unit a good first investment property?

answer.quote: I will not get it mainly because I have better options.
answer.summary: It is a very safe deal she can afford, and she wouldn't lose money. But Sean wouldn't buy it himself, because the same budget can buy newer units with more room to grow. With no rush, she should negotiate harder and compare all four buying channels first.

reasons.title: The rent already covers the loan
reasons.body: A RM400,000 loan over 35 years at 4% costs about RM1,800 to RM1,900 a month, around RM2,000 with maintenance, so today's RM2,200 rent breaks even. It could also let to families, medium-term tenants or students room by room, and Sean's rule is that the more ways a unit can cover its instalment, the better.

reasons.title: Old buildings protect the bottom, not the upside
reasons.body: Across the road, newer Bukit Jalil projects transact at RM900 to RM1,000 per sq ft and some rent for far more. A new building next door underpins an old one's value, but the old one rarely doubles. Sean treats buildings over ten years old as their own category, with their own median price.

reasons.title: Subsale takes real cash
reasons.body: She would need about RM45,500 down and about RM36,000 more for legal and other costs. Sean's own test is to have RM50,000 for renovation plus six months of instalments left over after buying.

reasons.title: The location is strong
reasons.body: Bukit Jalil has a KL address, quick roads to the city, rail links and private universities, which Sean believes keep students living nearby after they graduate. Families from older wealthy areas nearby also help their children buy apartments there.

actions: Before any investment, have six months of expenses as an emergency fund, medical insurance and a clear career path.
Negotiate: offer the price you would be happy with, such as RM400,000, and walk away if the owner refuses.
Compare what the same budget buys through new launch, subsale, auction and bulk purchase.
Compare an older unit's price with the median for older buildings, and a new one's with the median for new buildings.
If you buy, fully furnish the unit so it can be let in every way, from families to room by room.
articles.caveat: If she values certainty and knows the building well, buying it is not wrong: Sean calls it an awesome deal and a very safe route. The only regret would be watching newer projects nearby grow faster over ten to 15 years.

articles.title: Cheap old house or new house with no down payment?
articles.excerpt: An unmarried couple must choose between a cheap 30-year-old house needing renovation and a new one with a bigger instalment. Sean says the real question is whose income the loan depends on.

question.asker: From Winston, a viewer who wrote in by email
question.context: Winston, 34, works in Seremban; his girlfriend, 31, works in KL and does not want to give up her KL salary. They are not yet married, have RM400,000 in savings and earn about RM9,000 a month between them. After viewing more than 12 houses they have two options: a 30-year-old house in a convenient spot for RM338,000 at about RM1,500 a month, needing around RM200,000 for deposit, renovation and furniture; or a new house with zero down payment at about RM3,000 a month.
question.text: Should they spend most of their savings on the old house with the easy instalment, or take the new house with little cash upfront but double the monthly commitment?

answer.quote: You clearly cannot afford the bigger house.
answer.summary: Take the old house, and buy it in one name. On one income, a RM3,000 instalment is out of reach, and counting on a partner who has not committed to living in Seremban is the real risk.

reasons.title: Do not borrow on income you cannot count on
reasons.body: Sean discourages unmarried couples from buying in joint names; some split up before construction even finishes. Split evenly, each earns about RM4,500. That carries RM1,500 a month easily, but RM3,000 only works if she stays in, and she is not yet sure she will.

reasons.title: Compare with the area median, not the new house
reasons.body: RM338,000 against RM700,000 is the wrong comparison. What matters is recent prices in the same taman: if similar houses sold for around RM400,000, RM338,000 is a good buy; at market price it is fine. Just never pay above market without a clear reason.

reasons.title: Renovation does not add its cost to the value
reasons.body: A RM338,000 house plus RM200,000 of renovation is not a RM538,000 house. Valuers look at approved built-up area, such as extended kitchens and bedrooms with approved plans, not at marble or premium finishes. Unapproved extensions can even stop a future buyer getting a loan.

reasons.title: An old house is as good as how it was lived in
reasons.body: A house lived in continuously is usually fine, because problems get fixed as they appear. One left empty for five to ten years needs far more work, as seals and pipes crack once used again. Older layouts, with a staircase in the middle, also feel tighter than new designs.

actions: Agree on the life plan first: where you will both live, and how the household will work after marriage.
Buy in your own name, on your own income; your partner can contribute if she chooses.
Check recent transacted prices in the same taman before making an offer.
Bring a contractor to a second viewing, ask how long the house was empty, and get two or three quotations itemised space by space.
Do the necessities first: structure, wiring, plumbing, roof and toilets. Leave the nice-to-haves until your finances allow.
articles.caveat: If you are married, both committed to Seremban and investing together, the question changes. It becomes whether the RM200,000 would earn more invested elsewhere than the extra RM1,500 a month the new house costs, which Sean leaves for another episode.
articles.sourceNote: Summarised from Sean's full English captions for Asking Sean #242. The quoted answer is verbatim; everything else is paraphrased. Prices are as stated in February 2024.

articles.title: Should I buy my own place, or wait until I can afford it?
articles.excerpt: A 34-year-old in oil and gas earns RM11,000 but has only months of savings and likes a new PJ project costing RM3,000 a month. Sean says it is that unit she cannot afford, not property.

question.asker: From Miss L, a viewer who wrote in on Instagram
question.context: Miss L is 34 and works in oil and gas, where restructuring is common. She lives in her brother's condo and pays about RM1,500 a month towards its costs; he is now jobless, with a wife and young child. She earns about RM11,000, or RM8,500 net, but after her car, her parents' allowance and her credit card has RM1,500 to RM2,000 left, three to four months of savings and no investments. A new PJ project she likes would cost about RM3,000 a month including maintenance.
question.text: Should she buy that unit for own stay or investment, keep renting, or do something else?

answer.quote: It's not because the market is not ready. You are not ready.
answer.summary: Not now. Her income qualifies for a loan, but what is left each month cannot carry a RM3,000 commitment. Stay put, build savings and income, and when ready, buy a cheaper unit for investment first while she still values flexibility.

reasons.title: It's that unit she can't afford
reasons.body: Banks see RM11,000; they don't see that only about RM2,000 is left after expenses. At RM3,000 a month before renovation and insurance, the PJ unit is out of reach, but a RM300,000 to RM400,000 unit at about RM1,350 to RM1,800 a month would not be.

reasons.title: Savings are the real issue
reasons.body: Losing a job is out of her control; her savings are not. Sean's test is RM50,000 to RM60,000 for the makeover plus six months of costs: about RM68,000 in hand at key collection for a RM3,000-a-month unit.

reasons.title: The RM1,500 is cheap rent
reasons.body: What she pays her brother is cheap rent, and while he is jobless it means far more to him than it would to a landlord. Unless living together is straining things, staying helps him, and she shouldn't ask for the money back.

reasons.title: Single means flexible
reasons.body: Without children she does not need the certainty of her own home, and renting from owners whose units lose money is her best arrangement for now. Sean does encourage women to own an investment unit of their own, rented out until it is needed.

actions: Ask a bank how much you can borrow, using your payslip and EPF statement.
Visit 20 properties within that range, without booking anything.
Build your emergency fund before committing to any purchase.
Work out how to earn RM500 to RM1,000 more a month from your professional skills, not a second job.
When ready, buy for investment first, in a price range where the rent can cover the instalment.
articles.caveat: If she is set on that unit, Sean says it can work if she grows her income and has the savings in place by the time the keys are handed over. And once marriage and children come, the certainty of an own-stay home matters more.
articles.sourceNote: Summarised from Sean's full English captions for Asking Sean #299. The quoted answer is verbatim; everything else is paraphrased. Figures are as stated in October 2025.

articles.title: I'm in my 70s. What should my daughter do with our paid-off house?
articles.excerpt: A mother in her 70s has mapped out what her daughter should do with their landed home after she passes. Sean explains why cash and careful plans may not serve the next generation.

question.asker: From Madam X, a viewer who wrote in by email
question.context: Madam X is in her 70s and still teaches private tuition. She and her daughter, in her late 20s, own a freehold landed home in an upmarket area worth about RM1.3 million, bought with a 95% down payment, and keep a flexi loan and some cash for emergencies. The daughter earns about RM3,000 a month plus RM500 from a part-time job, and should clear the remaining loan in about eight years.
question.text: Is it sensible for the daughter, after her mother has passed away, to rent out the house for about RM3,000, buy a RM300,000 to RM350,000 condo near work, and do her own repairs to save money?

answer.quote: Simple life does not come cheap.
answer.summary: Sean wouldn't lock the daughter into a plan. She could simply keep living in the house, and should first work out what she wants; if she does invest, a loan works better than cash, and she should buy as soon as a unit's rent covers its instalment rather than wait.

reasons.title: Cash loses value faster than it seems
reasons.body: Official inflation is about 2.3%, but Sean puts his own at 10 to 11% a year, and fixed deposits pay only around 2%. He suggests keeping three to six months of expenses as an emergency fund and putting the rest into assets you understand.

reasons.title: Property bought in cash is a weak investment
reasons.body: NAPIC data shows landed homes across Malaysia rising about 2 to 3% a year on average, less than EPF or blue chips have returned. Property is also slow to turn into cash: even after you agree a sale, the money takes about six months to arrive.

reasons.title: Property pays when you borrow
reasons.body: It is one of the few assets you can buy with up to 90% financing. The daughter could refinance the paid-off house, or take a loan on a RM300,000 condo now if its rent covers the instalment, and use her savings elsewhere. Sean counts insurance as part of the cost, so loans don't become a burden on the family.

reasons.title: Let the next generation choose
reasons.body: A carefully planned portfolio can become a burden if a child's life goes elsewhere. Sean would rather parents act as the safety net while children find their own goals, and says that time spent earning more is often better than saving on plumbers and electricians.

actions: Keep three to six months of expenses as an emergency fund, and invest the rest in assets you understand, such as index funds, EPF or ASB.
If you buy property to invest, use a loan rather than cash, and count insurance as part of the cost.
Buy an investment unit only if its rent covers the instalment; if it does, there is no need to wait.
Let your children decide what they want before handing them a plan or a property portfolio.
Pay professionals for repairs if your time can earn more than their fee.
articles.caveat: If the daughter has no wish to invest, Sean says she needn't sell or rent out the house at all: she can stay on and avoid new commitments while she builds her career.
articles.sourceNote: Summarised from Sean's full English captions for Asking Sean #314. The quoted answer is verbatim; everything else is paraphrased. Figures are as stated in June 2026.

video.title: ASKING SEAN #314 | LEAVING MORE THAN JUST PROPERTY BEHIND

articles.title: Should parents buy property for their children?
articles.excerpt: Some parents pay the down payment on their children's homes; some children ask for their parents' EPF. Sean explains when help teaches responsibility, and when it breeds entitlement.

question.context: Parents who bought homes decades ago, such as a PJ terrace bought for RM120,000 and now worth about RM1.2 million, can afford to help their children buy at today's prices. Sean has heard from children who resent paying for a home their parents chose, and from one who wanted his parents to withdraw their EPF for his second home.
question.text: Should parents buy property for their children, and should children ask them to?

answer.quote: Be accountable for whatever decisions that you make.
answer.summary: Parents can help, but use it to teach: pay the down payment and let the child pay the instalments, as savings for the future. Children should stand on their own feet; borrowing a sum and repaying it is fine, but asking for parents' savings to invest is not.

reasons.title: Paying the instalment teaches responsibility
reasons.body: A friend earning RM4,000 to RM5,000 and living with his parents had a unit bought in his name, the parents paying the down payment. Already paying close to RM2,000 a month for a car, he resented the instalment, but it taught him that commitments must be paid.

reasons.title: Handouts breed entitlement
reasons.body: Sean knows a family where each of six children was given a home. They had no idea what their RM1.6 million semi-D costs, about RM5,000 to RM6,000 a month over 35 years, and came across as arrogant.

reasons.title: Parents' savings aren't yours to risk
reasons.body: If you want your parents' EPF, ask whether you can promise them the 5.5% to 6% a year it earns. Rates, bank rules and government policy can all change, and if the deal fails, the loss falls on their retirement.

reasons.title: Know what a home costs to carry
reasons.body: Sean's rule of thumb: every RM100,000 of loan costs about RM500 a month over 30 years, so a RM1 million condo means RM5,000 a month and an income near RM15,000. A peer on RM6,000 who owns one is most likely being helped.

actions: Parents: if you help, explain why, and present the property as long-term savings rather than a gift.
Children: if you borrow from your parents, borrow a fixed sum and repay it with interest once you can.
Don't ask parents to withdraw EPF or other retirement savings to fund your investment.
Buy within your own means, using the RM500-per-RM100,000 rule to check the instalment.
articles.caveat: For very wealthy families, Sean says it is a different conversation. And many young people now would rather have cash for a business or other ventures than a property bought for them.
articles.sourceNote: Summarised from Sean's full English captions for this November 2019 episode. The quoted answer is verbatim; everything else is paraphrased. The captions are unclear in places, so only clearly stated points are included.

articles.title: My parents will pay half. Must I buy a home to live in?
articles.excerpt: A first-time investor's parents will pay half the price, but only for a home to live in. Sean explains how to protect a one-income household and handle the condition.

question.asker: From Lim, a viewer who wrote in by email
question.context: Lim works in airline healthcare and takes home about RM4,500 a month. She is the household's breadwinner while her husband builds his business. She has RM37,000 in savings and RM19,000 in stocks, and her parents will give the couple RM50,000. She wants to invest in property for passive income, but her parents would rather she buy a home to live in, and have offered to pay half its price.
question.text: Is her money enough, or too risky while her husband's business is unstable? Should she buy new or subsale, and how should she handle her parents' condition?

answer.quote: Keep your money in your savings.
answer.summary: Protect your savings while the household runs on one income, and accept your parents' help graciously. Buy through a channel that needs little cash, and if the condition is a home, choose one that would still rent well.

reasons.title: Her savings are the household's safety net
reasons.body: With one income supporting the family, savings should cover about six months of expenses. Sean's principle is to own property using as little of your own money as possible. On RM4,500, an instalment of about RM1,500 supports a property of roughly RM300,000 to RM380,000.

reasons.title: Subsale and auction need too much cash
reasons.body: A subsale needs about 18% of the price upfront, around RM90,000 on RM500,000, before renovation, which itself costs RM38,000 to RM80,000 for a basic condo. Auction deposits of 5 to 10% are forfeited if the loan fails, and hidden problems such as unpaid fees or title issues make auctions unsuitable for first-timers.

reasons.title: New launches and bulk deals need the least cash
reasons.body: Developers clear leftover units by selling them in bulk to investor groups at 20 to 30% off, sometimes more, because open discounts would anger earlier buyers. Sean buys this way; two such units each pay him around RM1,200 to RM2,500 a month after costs, and the cash back can fund renovation.

reasons.title: Half the price is generous, with strings
reasons.body: Find out the limit (RM300,000? RM500,000?), the intent (most likely that their daughter always has a home of her own), whether they will want a say on location, and whether her husband is comfortable with it. Then judge the home as if you paid full price, because with half paid upfront almost anything looks cash-flow positive.

actions: Keep your savings as an emergency fund, and put the RM50,000 gift in fixed deposits or EPF until there is a plan.
Work out your loan limit, then visit about 20 properties in that range across buying channels.
As a first-timer, skip auction properties.
Ask your parents openly what their offer covers and whether conditions come with it, and discuss it with your spouse.
If you buy a home, choose one whose rent would cover about 85% of the full instalment, so you can rent it out when you move.
articles.caveat: Whether to accept help is personal; Sean says he would rather succeed without his parents' money, but there is no right or wrong. If you decline, the low-cash bulk purchase route still works. Note too that Malaysia's small down payments are unusual: many countries expect around 25%.
articles.sourceNote: Summarised from Sean's full English captions for Asking Sean #318. The quoted answer is verbatim; everything else is paraphrased. Sean buys bulk-purchase units through FAR Capital as a paying client, not as its owner. Figures are as stated in August 2026.

articles.title: Our family bought units through a property guru. How do we get out?
articles.excerpt: A viewer's parents bought several units through a property guru at the 2018 peak and now pay thousands a month to hold them. Sean explains how the scheme worked and how to decide what to sell.

question.asker: From Miss C, a viewer who wrote in on Instagram
question.context: Miss C is 34. In 2017 and 2018 her parents followed property gurus and bought several units at marked-up prices, through compressed loans and with cash back that has since disappeared. The loans are in her and her mother's names, and most carry no MRTA. Her mother, 65 and seriously ill, uses her EPF to cover about RM6,000 to RM7,000 a month after rent. Selling now means a loss, and her father refuses to sell the family's landed house. Miss C has fully paid one unit of her own.
question.text: How deep is the trouble, and what can the family do when selling most of the units means taking a loss?

answer.quote: You are in a bad situation, but not the worst.
answer.summary: Bad, but recoverable. Put every unit into one table to see which can be sold and which must be held, and ask her father to refinance the family house for a standby credit line instead of selling it.

reasons.title: The cash back was never spare money
reasons.body: Guru deals came with large cash back, meant to pay for renovation and to cover the negative cash flow until the next upturn. Sean says many buyers spent it instead and forgot it was borrowed money they still pay interest on.

reasons.title: Compressed loans hid the real risk
reasons.body: Buyers applied for several similar units with different banks at the same time, so the credit system read it as one buyer comparing rates, and all the loans went through. Sean says the system now records each property's address, so this no longer works, but the debt taken on then remains.

reasons.title: A table shows which units to release
reasons.body: Compare each unit's outstanding loan with its current selling price, and its rent with its instalment and maintenance. Where the loan is close to the selling price, sell to exit. Where the rent covers the instalment, hold. Where a sale would still need a top-up, hold unless you can afford the difference.

reasons.title: Without cover, debt passes to the family
reasons.body: With no MRTA, the loans fall on the family rather than being cleared if the borrower dies. Sean says the point of property investing is to help the family, so every loan should come with mortgage cover such as MRTA or MLTA.

actions: List every unit with its outstanding loan, current market price, instalment plus maintenance, and rent, and update the list every quarter.
Sell the units whose loan is close to their selling price, and hold those whose rent already covers the instalment.
Refinance a fully owned home for an overdraft rather than selling it. On a RM1 million house at 60%, that is about RM600,000 of standby credit, charged daily only on what you use.
Rent out any unit you own outright and live with family for now; Sean estimates RM1,000 to RM2,000 a month to put towards the shortfall.
Give each unit to an agent who specialises in that area, instead of one company for all of them, which may sit on the listings.
articles.caveat: The sell-or-hold rules assume the family can keep paying while they wait; if no one can cover the shortfall, losses have to be taken sooner. Sean also points out that the parents' own savings, which the message doesn't mention, could change the picture.
articles.sourceNote: Summarised from Sean's full English captions for Asking Sean #296. The quoted answer is verbatim; everything else is paraphrased. Figures are as Sean stated them in September 2025; his rough estimate of the portfolio's total debt is left out.

articles.title: How do you know a project is not overpriced?
articles.excerpt: Projects borrow the name of a famous neighbourhood to charge its prices. Sean walks through the research that shows what an address is really worth.

question.context: Most buyers research a property by scrolling a listings portal. Developers know it, and borrow the name of a famous neighbourhood: projects next to Mont Kiara or Dutamas market themselves as part of it. Buyers end up paying the famous address's price without getting its tenants or its rents.
question.text: What research do you need to do to know whether a project is priced right?

answer.quote: We got to know the location inside out.
answer.summary: Go beyond the listing. Work out where the real neighbourhood ends, which tier of tenant it attracts, and compare the project only against like-for-like transacted prices: new against new, old against old, in the same tier.

reasons.title: A borrowed name does not bring borrowed rents
reasons.body: In June 2024, older projects in the Dutamas area averaged RM538 per sq ft outside Dutamas proper against RM818 inside it, and newer ones about RM641 against roughly RM1,070. Five minutes apart, the tenants and the premiums they will pay are completely different.

reasons.title: Know which tier you are buying into
reasons.body: Tier 1 areas such as Mont Kiara, Dutamas, KLCC and Bangsar South draw expatriates and have no real ceiling on rent. Tier 2 areas such as TTDI and Kota Damansara attract well-off locals; prices per sq ft can be similar, but rents hit a ceiling. Tier 3 is further out, with landed homes under RM500,000.

reasons.title: Compare new with new and old with old
reasons.body: At the same rent, about 95% of tenants will choose the newer unit, so buying new at an old unit's price is close to a sure win. For older Dutamas projects, the session suggested not paying above RM700 per sq ft, or RM550 in the surrounding areas.

reasons.title: Make sure two rental plans break even
reasons.body: Whole-unit leases, short stays and room-by-room rental each suit different tiers. Sean's one-plus-one in Mont Kiara earns RM5,000 from a single tenant but would make about RM4,000 by the room. Short-stay occupancy data showed demand only in Dutamas and Mont Kiara proper.

actions: Walk the area and map where the real neighbourhood ends, whatever the project calls itself.
Pull recent transacted prices, not asking prices, and find the median for your tier, split into new and old.
Aim to buy below that median. Sean bought in Mont Kiara at about RM900 per sq ft, roughly 20% below completed transactions near RM1,100.
Before buying, confirm at least two ways of renting the unit that would each cover the instalment.
Visit the site: a portal cannot show you access roads, traffic or what is being built next door.
articles.caveat: The tier system and price ceilings come from research by FAR Capital, the deal-sourcing company Sean buys through as a paying member, presented in a June 2024 live session. They are a snapshot of one area; repeat the work for your own location rather than reusing the numbers.

articles.title: Which taxes do I pay when I own and sell property?
articles.excerpt: Beyond the price, owners pay stamp duty, assessment, quit rent and RPGT, and income tax decides whether you can borrow at all. Sean goes through the five.

question.context: Investors often work out their profit as the selling price minus the buying price. Sean says that leaves out five taxes that change what a property really costs and earns, and that young investors should understand them before buying.
question.text: Which taxes should a property buyer in Malaysia budget for?

answer.quote: You need proof that you have money to buy.
answer.summary: Five: stamp duty when you buy, assessment and quit rent every year you own it, RPGT when you sell at a gain, and income tax. For a young buyer, income tax matters first, because a declared income is the proof a bank lends on.

reasons.title: Declared income is what banks lend on
reasons.body: Under-declaring income saves tax but blocks loans; Sean has seen hawkers forced to borrow other people's names and payslips. Someone declaring RM36,000 a year won't get a loan for a RM500,000 house, and paying a large sum in cash instead can draw questions from the Inland Revenue Board.

reasons.title: Stamp duty comes twice, in cash
reasons.body: Buyers pay stamp duty on the transfer and again on the loan agreement, in cash, which surprises many first-time buyers. The transfer scale rises in bands from 1%; Sean uses about 2.5% of the price as a quick estimate.

reasons.title: Two taxes recur every year
reasons.body: Assessment tax (cukai pintu) goes to the local council for street lights, drains and rubbish collection, charged as a percentage of the rent the council sets, which varies by council and property type. Quit rent (cukai tanah) goes to the state, and strata owners pay it too.

reasons.title: Selling has its own rules
reasons.body: RPGT is charged on your gain when you sell, at rates the government changes to cool or warm the market, and foreigners pay more. Legal fees, agent fees and improvements can be deducted. Sell many properties quickly and the Inland Revenue Board may treat it as a business and tax the gain as income, which Sean puts at up to 24%.

actions: Declare your full income and pay tax on it, so you can prove to a bank what you earn.
Budget for stamp duty on both the transfer and the loan agreement as cash, on top of the down payment.
Include assessment and quit rent in your yearly holding costs.
Keep receipts for legal fees, agent fees and improvements to reduce RPGT when you sell; you can file it yourself rather than rely on the lawyer's figure.
If you trade several properties, space out your sales; Sean says some investors sell no more than one a year.
articles.caveat: The rates Sean mentions date from late 2019 and RPGT and stamp duty rules have changed since, so check the current ones. An owner who keeps one home for the long term may never face RPGT or the business-income rules.
articles.sourceNote: Summarised from Sean's full English captions for this December 2019 episode. The quoted answer is verbatim; everything else is paraphrased. The captions are unclear in places, so only clearly stated points are included, and tax rates have changed since 2019.
